Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening my preliminary remarks had reference to the outlook for the resources for tomorrow conference which is to be held next October. I was suggesting this would not only be a landmark in the history of this department but perhaps a springboard to the future. However, the point I -made earlier about the initiative and vigour of the minister was occasioned by the reaction I obtained from several people in the last few weeks on the resources for tomorrow conference.
Last week an editor of a prominent business magazine in Canada was talking to me. I asked him, "Why have you not mentioned the resources for tomorrow conference? I have not noticed any editorial comment or any indication at all of the conference." This editor of this prominent business magazine in Canada said "What conference?" I said, "The resources for tomorrow conference." I point out that these big flies in the main contain material on the conference that I picked up from the secretariat. Here was a man who has not heard of the conference. He was quite willing to accept the onus; he said he had just not heard of it. I ask the minister what kind of preparation he has made for the conference when a man in a position such as this has not even heard of it, and the program has been under way for two years. The preparation has been going on that long and we are having the conference this year.
This is shocking enough to me, but during the Easter vacation I was making a tour of my riding. I encountered the president of the district council, lumber and saw mill workers union, an organization that has approximately 11,000 people working in the bush just at this particular time. It is the strongest union in the woods in Ontario. It is a militant union that carries its organization right out into the bush. It is in constant negotiation and is having conflict with many of the companies, but it is recognized as a very able organization. I could refer the minister to any number of articles in various magazines such as Business Week, Saturday Night and Executive, all dealing with the impact of this union upon this great resource industry in Ontario.
I said to the president of this particular union, "Who is going from your union to the resources for tomorrow conference?". His reply was "What conference?". I said, "The resources for tomorrow conference". He said "I have not heard anything about it. I vaguely know there is some such thing going on, but I have not heard anything about it". I said "Surely you had an invitation". He said "No". I said "Have you considered that you might perhaps get together with the I.W.A. and the Catholic union in Quebec? After all, labour


is a very important part of this greatest industry we have in Canada?" He said, "It is funny; I was talking to Mr. Ladd of I.W.A. not so long ago. He did not mention anything about it. I doubt whether he has heard much about it or had any invitation".
My point is that here is an indication that this fundamental conference, which could be a springboard to the future, is really unknown by people who should have an intimate relationship with it and, so far as the labour people are concerned, should be playing a very active part in it. This is one of the disappointments about the papers that are listed in the information bulletin No. 1. There is no indication here that organized labour is playing any real part in this conference; yet wherever one turns to hear about the problems of Canada today in the export trade

and that is where our resources industries concentrate-the accusation or the criticism is often made that our wage policy is pricing us out of this trade or market, or we have not the labour where we need it; we do not have labour mobility.
It does seem strange that one should project a conference of this importance, spend a whole lot of money on it and two years in its preparation, have a secretariat that is spending a fair amount of money and giving a fair amount of leadership, and not get the information out to places and to people who could take a more positive role.
Having said that, I do not want to leave the impression that I think the basic work of the secretariat has not been sound. I have heard from provincial sources that the whole plan of the conference did not crystallize in any dynamic way until the new minister from Quebec came to the fore. I am referring to Mr. Rene Levesque. Without commenting upon Mr. Levesque's politics, I think it is about the most exciting news that anyone with interest in resources could hear that the minister from Quebec was prepared to come in, and not just drag along but to give leadership in putting this conference upon a realistic basis. I think praise cannot be too great for something like this. I know that we need such leadership in Ontario, because there is a tendency for our people in the resources field to slumber along and look at Ontario more as a little nation of our own in a resource sense rather than as an integral part of the nation. If we can be complimentary for a contribution that has been made, we would like to give that support to Mr. Rene Levesque.
Last year when I raised a question about the resources for tomorrow conference I received a letter dated August 11, 1960 from

the then minister of northern affairs and national resources. The letter contains this statement:
To these official policy statements I would add that the conference is designed to put us-and by "us" I mean all participants-in a better judgment position in regard to the many related questions of land and water use and the conservation and development of resources in all their ramifications. It is intended to bring out for discussion all the known facts in this connection through research papers-
Then the letter goes on:
We cannot, of course, expect the conference-given its composition-to be able to decide or even to be able to recommend clearly upon action. But we will all without any doubt be in a better position after the conference to make informed decisions about how to improve the use of our renewable resources, so that the nation can draw a higher income from them without prejudicing the supply.
Later we find this remark in the letter:
The question of foreign ownership of capital will be considered indirectly in reviewing the sources of capital for resource development. Perhaps the conference will suggest how best to channel Canadian funds into resource development.
Now, I did ask the minister whether there was any intention of dealing with cost-benefit analysis in this conference, which is a need we have at the present time in order to get resources development. The minister's answers to questions earlier in the session indicated that cost-benefit analysis will be incidental. There are several papers that touch upon that subject and I was delighted to see that according to the schedule the second part of the conference program will include two workshops dealing with capital requirements, income and employment effects. The conference will conclude in plenary session on Saturday, October 28, with a session dealing with capital requirements, income and employment effects of renewable resources development.
This is not the time, Mr. Chairman, for any kind of philosophical analysis. However, as one who believes that planning or democratic socialism is the only future for Canada and the Canadian economy, I recognize that this conference and the approach to it is a step in that direction. For that reason we are enthusiastic about it.
This year the government created something like a national planning board, in effect, with Mr. George DeYoung as its head, called the national productivity council. I should like to ask the minister whether arrangements have been made to have the members of this council attend the resources for tomorrow conference. There is not much purpose in having an esoteric discussion unless there is liaison or some means of carrying out the recommendations and ideas that come forward in the conference. For that
Supply-Northern Affairs reason I should like to know just how much effort is to be made by this national productivity council to work with the conference and the conference secretariat.
There is another question I should like to discuss with the minister. What steps are being planned to see that the initiative that comes from the conference is not lost or dissipated? Is any consideration being given to a continuing secretariat or to making the secretariat a part of the national productivity council? It seems to me there is a very direct relationship here. I would very much welcome any information in that regard that the minister can give.
Referring to another aspect of the minister's responsibilities, I might say that in looking at the map on pages 34 and 35 of the annual report I was astounded to see that one of the roads projected there seems to run from somewhere in my constituency near Armstrong or Nipigon all the way up into northern Manitoba. I have had given to me by the minister a return dealing with the roads in northern Ontario which have been approved. I just cannot match the roads shown in the return with those shown on the map. I should like to ask the minister whether approval has been given for the complete length of the road which is shown by a dotted line running from near lake Nipigon all the way up into northern Manitoba, or whether this represents a survey only. I certainly would like to argue that in time we will need that kind of road to open up that area. However, I have not received any impression from the information I have been given that such a road is a sure thing or that the whole business has been confirmed.
I might repeat to the minister something that he has heard from a number of other members in the last few years. I am sure that one of the great disillusionments with the Diefenbaker government stems from the feeling of people in areas such as I represent, in which we have always talked about our unlimited resources, our untapped resources. They know that these lie much closer to the markets and industries of North America, and when they find that the great northern vision is prematurely focusing on the wrong places, the disillusion is immense. After all, when you have very large iron ore resources in northern Ontario; great forest resources that are still not exploited; when you have oil wells and gas wells capped in Alberta; when within 100 or 120 miles of the border you have all these natural resources that are not being exploited although these areas have been built on optimistic hopes for the future, it comes as quite a shock to have the northern vision put to you at a time when you are languishing yourself. I can only say to the

Supply-Northern Affairs minister that this does not mean that I or anyone else would suggest to him that the responsibilities of the department in this field should be allowed to lapse. I suggest to him that if the northern vision became a southern vision it would probably have a more beneficial effect for the Diefenbaker government in the long run.
Another point upon which I wanted to touch very briefly, Mr. Chairman, concerns one sentence in the annual report of the department. This sentence refers to the standard of living, buildings and morale in the Mackenzie river area as exceedingly low. I think that is the phrase, "exceedingly low". Certain steps are being taken to correct the situation, and I should like to hear from the minister. Here we have a statement as it was provided late last year. I should like to hear from the minister why this is so.
Perhaps the hon. member for Yukon can provide us with the answer. The government has been in power now for four years, or approximately that period of time. We have had this department of northern affairs for a much longer time than that. Yet we have been told that morale is exceedingly low in a very important sector of the minister's responsibility, and it is acknowledged in the annual report. I like this kind of frankness, but I should like to have some documentation as to the reasons and to have a little more information as to the steps that are being taken to change the situation.
I have often felt that frequently parliamentary committees make recommendations that fall away and just disappear. One of the things I should like the minister to provide for me and other members who may be interested, after the minister's estimates are through, is an appraisal of all recommendations that have been made with regard to his department by parliamentary committees, and the consideration that has been given to them. I think this may be something that the committee itself should expect. I see no reason why we should not know.
I may have been off base last night in expressing the suggestion that this department had been the one most criticized by parliamentary committees. However, whether or not I was off base, I know that many criticisms have been made. Having regard to the criticisms and the recommendations, I should like to know what consideration has been given to them by the department and where they stand at the present time. As someone who took part in the deliberations of the committee for a considerable portion of the time, may I suggest that it would bring into some kind of focus what we were doing.

I should hope we could get through the minister's estimates without getting off into any bitter avenues such as those which were revealed here last night in relation to the fact that French is not taught to the Eskimos in northern Quebec. The minister gave us the information that 90 per cent, I think it was, of the children in this particular area are in the Anglican church. The only suggestion I can make to the committee as a teacher is that it is difficult enough to teach children coming from a culture or a civilization that is not as steady or as stable as our own without getting into the question of teaching two foreign languages or having to operate within three languages. I can say this with absolute conviction because, despite the fact that I took French for eight or nine years in school myself, all I can do is read it; I would not have the temerity to try to speak it.

DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks before the first item of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is carried.
I shall avail myself of this opportunity to thank the minister sincerely for the explanations he gave yesterday, and more particularly to underline the fact that, as he said himself in his statement, his first formal duty when he became minister was the signing of the agreement between the government of Canada which he was representing on that occasion, and the provincial government of Quebec, represented by the Hon. Paul Earl, then minister of mines for the province, when the province of Quebec participated in the roads to resources program. It gives me pleasure to stress the fact, as the three roads which were the object of that understanding will be jointly built by the federal and provincial governments, with the federal government paying 50 per cent of the total building costs.
These three roads are within the limits of Chapleau riding, which I have the honour to represent in this house.
The minister also was kind enough to explain the proposed program in a general way, or at least the various divisions under his
Supply-Northern Affairs department. I should like to mention briefly in that respect, a few points which concern his department.
I shall now briefly describe the three roads I mentioned and which are to be built in the northern part of Chapleau riding. I have here a copy of the agreement signed in Quebec on October 19, 1960, which is very elaborate. I have no intention, of course, to read it fully into the official record, but I should like, if I may, Mr. Chairman, to give a description of those roads, as they are located within the boundary of my riding.
First of all, there is the road between Amos and Mattagami, a distance of approximately 118 miles. This is a new road. Some sections were started and even completed a few years ago, but they had to be widened or improved. This road goes northward from Amos, up to the Mattagami lake district, or more accurately to the Allard river, where a mining company owns a very interesting property, the New Hosco mine. That road will also serve other mines in the Mattagami lake district, like the Mattagami Lake Mines, the Orchan Mines and other mining companies which have been doing some exploratory work since 1956 in that area, which is about 100 miles to the north of the town of Amos.
The second road is a section, or a new road, should I say, leading from lake Waconi-chi to lake Albanel, to the north of the Chapais and Chibougamau region. The new road, 95 miles long, will stretch up to a few miles beyond the 51st parallel, on the eastern shore of lake Albanel, that is to the east of that lake, an area where vast iron deposits have already been discovered. Indeed, the whole area around Albanel lake and great Mistassini lake offers immense mining opportunities.
The third stretch is the road between the cities of Chapais and Desmaraisville.
In addition, in the northern part of the constituency, a 30-mile stretch will link up southern Abitibi with the northern part of the area.
For many years, or at least since the area of Chapais and Chibougamau was opened up, about 10 years ago, there was no connection between the two sections of that part of our area. As a result, people had to travel either by air or by road, covering over 1,000 miles, depending on where they started from in the Abitibi area. Needless to say this road will be a tremendous boon, as it will shorten the distance between the Abitibi and the Chapais and Chibougamau area to ap-

Supply-Northern Affairs proximately 200 miles, depending of course on the particular starting point in the Abitibi.
A fourth item of interest to the province of Quebec, in the federal-provincial agreement, provides as follows:
Resource development roads in various sections of the province, the location of which will be determined by the provincial minister, subject to written approval by the minister.
This refers of course, to future roads planned for northern Quebec. I shall therefore be brief on this subject.
However, I felt it was my duty, as representative of the Chapleau constituency, to mention those three stretches of road. One of them is already under construction, between Amos and Mattagami, while the others are to be built shortly, as soon as the provincial authorities can get around to it, because the federal government has agreed to contribute as its share up to 50 per cent of construction costs.
Another program of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is of particular interest to my constituents and myself. I refer to hydrometric studies, that is to say the study of water streams in James bay, north of Barraute and Senneterre, where important mining developments are under way and where a railroad is also being constructed.
The streams being surveyed in the James bay basin are the Bell or Nottaway, Broad-back, Rupert and Eastmain rivers.
This study is being conducted jointly by the federal and provincial authorities. The work was started a couple of years ago, and the provincial government is at the same time making a survey of possible hydraulic resources in those rivers.
I understand that the survey program is still going on and that an office was opened by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in Senneterre in 1958 or 1959, from which the people working on the survey start off in the spring, after the thaw-out.
Another scheme was also placed before the committee of mines, forests and waters last year.
I asked a question to the minister during this session concerning the Grand Canal project, as it is called in English. That project concerns the Harricanaw river.
I think that is a problem the department should be seriously considering. It should have a complete survey made of the possibilities, in order to decide whether the project would be self-sustaining in the years to come.
[Mr. Martel.l
We all know that in the southern United States, there is a problem of fresh water supply, whose solution may dangerously affect the situation in Canada, since the authorities of the state of Illinois or of Chicago are planning to divert the waters of lake Michigan. In fact, such diversion would channel lake Michigan waters into the Mississippi basin.
Of course this is an international problem, which will require the co-operation of the United States. If there were an increase in the volume of water already diverted into the Mississippi basin, south of Chicago, this will seriously affect the Great lakes, as was explained last year in the committee of mines, forests and waterways. Furthermore, that diversion would be detrimental to navigation on the St. Lawrence seaway.
Again I say this is not only an international problem but a national one. We know that if navigation on the St. Lawrence seaway is threatened or curtailed, our trade will considerably suffer as a result.
Consequently, I think it would be in order to make a complete survey of fresh water supply diverted into James bay and to the north, in view of the urgent need which might develop in the coming years, both in the United States, particularly in those states bordering on Canada, and in this country too, in the Great lakes area.
We know that the southern United States are fast becoming industralized.
I believe that when the survey is completed, we shall be in a position to establish exactly not only the fresh water needs of those states, but also the dangers involved in the diversion of more water through Chicago or south of Chicago.
Again I say that such diversion would affect the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway.
Consequently, if there is a possibility of using the fresh water running into James bay, it would perhaps be wise-I think, for my part, the project is really worth studying-that we should start working on it and try to solve it as soon as possible.
Besides, I think the department has already set up an observation post to measure the volume of water on the Harricanaw river, at Amos, and the statistics that have been compiled for several years may help survey work northward up to the mouth of that river.
Before closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment on some remarks made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. APRIL 21, 1961
Deschatelets), especially when he tried to suggest that the credit for northern vision should not necessarily be claimed by the Conservative government, but rather by the former minister of northern affairs and national resources who is now premier of the province of Quebec.
It is quite possible; I was not a member of parliament in 1953, as was the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont. However, he overlooked one point and it is this: if the former minister of northern affairs and national resources was already possessed of that northern vision, as he says, the government of the time certainly did not believe him. It was only when the Conservative government came into power that the program he was then advocating, or at least the development of northern areas was applied.
I am not afraid of saying now that, with the present minister, we are on the right course and that people up north are delighted at the greater consideration they are getting from this government.
Another point I wish to emphasize is that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefen-baker) is quite conversant with northern problems. This is something I have mentioned during the last two election campaigns, in 1957 and in 1958.
In fact, the Prime Minister has never resided anywhere but in the northern part of this country; he knows the problems of northern Canada and he will no doubt be the best prime minister the people of the north will ever have had, because he knows their problems and tries to find practical solutions for them.
I will now close my remarks, Mr. Chairman. I may have further comment to make, but I will wait until the detailed discussion of the department's estimates.

Before embarking on a discussion of the minister's estimates I should like to thank him and the officials of his department for the co-operation they have given me last year and, indeed, during the whole of the time I have been here. Every suggestion I have made to them has been carefully considered, and I am very grateful to them and to the minister. I should like to express the gratitude of my constituents for the results that have been experienced, since the majority of the suggestions I have put forward have been accepted.
I intend to discuss the estimates of the department under three particular headings; the political development of the north in a non-partisan sense, the material development and the human development. But before doing that I want to comment on the remarks of the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, who spoke last night on the estimates of this department. Never have I heard so much drivel or so much senseless discussion concerning the north. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont did not make one constructive remark last night, not one accurate statement concerning those areas above the 60th parallel. He made all sorts of show in producing submissions made to the Gordon commission by those two territories, and by quoting sketchy verbal excerpts from these representations the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont attempted to garner credit for his party for the tremendous increase in expenditure and activity which have occurred north of the 60th parallel since the present Prime Minister came to power.
The fact of the matter is that the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont does not know the north, and he is certainly not familiar with the activities of the department in the last three years. If he was, he would know that while the government which he supported was in office, in 1956-57 the

Supply-Northern Affairs estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources amounted to $39 million. If the hon. member were familiar with these things he would know that in the following year the estimates amounted to $53,700,000; these figures are approximate. He would also know that as soon as the government changed hands in 1958-59 the estimates of this department rose to $83 million.

Of course I am aware of it, Mr. Chairman. But the same story could be told about the estimates of the Department of Transport, the estimates of the Department of National Defence, the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare or, indeed, of any other federal government department which operates in the north. All of them have shown increases in their estimates in ratios comparable to those I am citing now. Activity has increased at least fivefold among all the federal departments in the north. It is very notable if one lives there. One cannot help but notice the difference between then and now.
I will continue the statistics I have been giving and tell the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont, in case he should have overlooked this, that in 1959-60 the estimates of the department jumped to $89,898,000-almost $90 million-and this year they amount to $81,500,000, though if forestry is added they amount, as the minister has told us, to $3 million more than last year. So that from 1956-57, when the estimates of the department stood at $40 million, they have increased to almost $100 million. In fact they have more than doubled, the figure standing at $90 million last year.
This is reflected in what one sees in the north as compared with what one did not see

in the past. I do not want to be unfair regarding what has been accomplished. There were accomplishments by the previous government in the north, and I will say that the accomplishments were misdirected. I will give credit to the previous government for initiating the Gordon commission study, because that study provided the basis for some of the planning that was done so matters could go ahead when the government took office. Do not forget, however, that the Gordon commission plan, such as it was in so far as roads and other developments in the north were concerned, was predicated on a 25-year program. That program has been consolidated and accelerated into a program for some five to ten years. I do not know the exact time that has been allotted to the program by the department, but undoubtedly the minister will enlighten us. It certainly has been accelerated a good deal.
As a result of living in the north myself I am able to enlighten the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont by telling him that a good many things have occurred in the north in the last three years under this government that do not appear in the Gordon commission report. In my own riding of Yukon, and the story can be duplicated in respect of the Northwest Territories, we have the construction of a new school at Dawson city, a new school and teacherage at Mayo Landing, a health centre at Haines Junction and Watson Lake, a new school at Whitehorse, two $1 million hostels at Whitehorse, a new school under construction at Whitehorse, a new federal building under construction at Dawson city and houses and apartments built for federal civil servants in the Whitehorse area, none of which appear in the Gordon commission report. There has been an amazing and beneficial change in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation legislation which has allowed building to proceed under that legislation in the Yukon where none was in existence before this government took office. Not one single unit was built previously under the National Housing Act in the Yukon, yet this year I anticipate there will be 50 to 70 units under construction or completed under N.H.A.
Let us focus the attention of this committee on the road program in the north. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont has attempted to garner credit for the plans of this government in connection with the road construction program now going ahead in the north for the development of our resources there. During the fiscal year 1957-58 some $3.8 million was spent on construction and development of roads in the north. In 1959-60 some $8.2 million was spent in this regard, and in 1960-61 the sum of $6.2 million was

spent. Included in the estimates of the department for this fiscal year is provision for an expenditure of $8.4 million. The average amount provided for this fundamental development purpose by the government is $6.5 million over these years. Contrasting this with the record of the previous administration, where the average was $1.5 million, I suggest to the hon. member that is a very telling comparison.
The attack by that hon. member last night regarding the Liberal planning program referred not to a planning program at all. The planning had to be done when the government changed, and that planning, I must say, has gone ahead, contrary to the opinion of the hon. member for Port Arthur, under the direction of the civil service staffing the department who are devoted, dedicated and altruists of the highest order. The deputy minister is a man who I consider the government, and that department particularly, is fortunate in having at the reins of this important department of government. I have not seen dedication like his for many years. I certainly hope that he stays with the department because I am sure, with his qualifications, the attractions for employment outside the government service must indeed be tempting.
I want to associate myself with only one remark made by the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont, on a matter introduced by the minister, and that is the wish that the hon. member for Mackenzie River will be back with us in this house within the shortest possible time to give us the benefit of his knowledge of the affairs of the Mackenzie river area.
I would point out one further discrepancy in the remarks made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont for which he can perhaps be excused, when he said last night and I use his words taken from page 7 of the translation appearing in last night's Hansard, as follows:
-farming is only possible in and around the Mackenzie district-
I would like to inform him that there is a good potential for agricultural development in the Yukon as well as in the Mackenzie district. In keeping abreast with developments in this regard I can tell him also that under the very able leadership of the Minister of Agriculture, who is extremely familiar with the problems confronting northern development, a committee has been set up of representatives from his department, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and other federal government departments, interested, for the specific purpose of assessing that agricultural potential in the Yukon and devising a method of land
Supply-Northern Affairs allotment so that the development can go ahead. I might say this is the first time that this sort of attack has been made in an endeavour to proced with the agricultural development in my riding.
I think the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur concerning the minister were quite deplorable. He said he was disappointed in the change of ministers. I might say that I was most disappointed that the hon. member for Port Arthur saw fit to be critical of the minister in this rather personal fashion. I certainly do not know this minister as well as I knew the previous minister, but since I have been in the house I have had several discussions with him, and must say that from my observations he has certainly been one of the most active and virile of the members taking part in the activities of this house.
I must say that this is contrary to an interview I read in the Toronto Telegram Week End magazine of July 16, 1960 with the hon. member for Port Arthur. According to that article the hon. member believes that too many parliamentary backbenchers often unwillingly, lead an aimless and frustrating existence as time-servers, merely voting "yea" or "nay" at the call of their party. The hon. member went on to say, according to the article, that he himself is so dissatisfied with life as a member of parliament that he intends to go back to teaching school after the next election is called. While I think this is perhaps-

I simply used the article to point out to the hon. member for Port Arthur that the industry displayed by the minister, certainly from my observation of his activities in the house, is not consistent with the views of the hon. member in respect of the activities or non-activities of most hon. members in this house. When it comes to taking part in activities in this house on behalf of my own

Supply-Northern Affairs constituents, I can tell the hon. member that I devote all my time to those activities.
Let me pass to the political development of the north. In this respect I believe that some considerable thought is about due. I am not suggesting for a moment that considerable thought has not already been given to this problem, but I think a concentrated second look at the political development of the north is required. I think I heard wrongly, or that the C.B.C. reported the minister wrongly during the Easter recess, when in a speech before the Yellowknife board of trade he was reported as advocating that the Yukon and the Mackenzie river districts could be best combined in order to create the eleventh province of Canada in due course. I do not believe the minister intended to say that. As a matter of fact I do not believe he did say it. Perhaps the C.B.C. had him all wrong on it.
Of course this is practically, politically, historically and geographically impossible in my view. I feel that the Yukon, with its traditions, its history, its geography and its economy must be created a province by itself when the time comes. I am not suggesting that that should be forthwith, but certainly the economic development seems to be progressing at a pace which makes this look possible within a decade.
Here again I must disagree with the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and other hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Welland, for one, the hon. member for Renfrew North for another and the Leader of the Opposition, for a third, who have been ridiculing the vision, and using the word "vision" with derision in their voices. Not one of them realizes the pace and the tempo that the north is feeling at the moment as a result of this government's activities there. As a direct result of the development road program there I can say that exploration activity has been increased to the point where we in Canada-I do not say we in the Yukon -have the world's largest known tungsten deposit, which was discovered in 1958 and which is slated for production in the fall of 1962. This is a strategic metal of great importance. Before this discovery we produced no tungsten in Canada. We will now be in a position to supply, for instance, the whole of the United States demand for tungsten. This discovery was the direct result of this development road program. Therefore I suggest to hon. members that they do not underestimate the benefit to the whole of Canada of the program which this government is following.
The minister will likely enlighten us on the statement reported by the C.B.C. concerning the combining of the Mackenzie district and

the Yukon. There are many reasons why such a suggestion is completely incompatible with practicality.
Another matter that I wish to raise for the minister's attention is the point that the Northwest Territories, as hon. members know, being divided into three districts, namely the Mackenzie river district, the Keewatin district and the Franklin district, is an extremely large area indeed. The hon. member for Mackenzie River has as his riding only the Mackenzie river district. The whole of the eastern mainland above the 60th parallel, the Keewatin district, and the whole of the Franklin district comprising all the Canadian archipelago and the islands of the far north, are without representation in the House of Commons. There are Canadian citizens disfranchised; civil servants, members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, missionaries and a substantial population in those two areas who should be entitled to be heard in this house. I have had correspondence from such organizations as the Baker Lake citizens association, who have asked that this be brought to the attention of hon. members so that some solution might be found.
In my view the solution does not lie in placing the responsibility for representing those people in the hands of the hon. member for Mackenzie River. He has his hands full now in representing his own vast area. I believe the solution lies in the creation of an additional electoral district to take in this area so that Canada may be truly 100 per cent represented. It certainly is not now when we have this vast area with, as I say, a substantial population without a member in this house.
I would also draw the attention of the minister to the fact that neither the Yukon nor the Northwest Territories has Senate representation. The solution of the problem here requires the amendment of the British North America Act in order to qualify the Yukon and the Northwest Territories for Senate representation. Both these matters were covered by bills which I introduced in the house last year. I would judge by the number of bills on the order paper this year it would be very unlikely that, should I introduce the legislation again this year, it would receive any consideration.
I feel that the department should attempt to extract from its very busy agenda some time to develop a political blueprint for the development of the north. It should develop a formula such as that which was developed when Manitoba was created a province in the years prior thereto. I am sure the minister, who remembers the history of his province, will recall the formula which was developed there. When the population increased by

2,000 an additional seat was added to the council. When the number totalled 20 or 21, 1 forget which, the council was converted into a full-fledged provincial legislature. Some such formula should be worked out for the Yukon territory so that when the economy of the Yukon does reach the stage where we are ready to take on the responsibility of a province, a blueprint will be there and we shall be following an organized course.
I am very grateful to the previous minister for following the suggestion which I put before him as soon as I came to the house of increasing the number of members of the Yukon legislative council from five to seven. This provided for more equitable representation on the legislative council in the Yukon and also enlarged the council so the minister could accept the suggestion of creating an advisory committee on finance, which will be formed after the next election in the territory this year. This advisory committee on finance is the first tottering step toward selfgovernment in the Yukon, in that the commissioner will now be obliged, mandatorily, to consult with the advisory committee before he prepares his budget.
I am sure hon. members realize that in the Yukon Territory the council is wholly elected, as contrasted with the Northwest Territories where four members of a nine-man council are elected and the other five are appointed by the federal government, so that in the Yukon we are substantially ahead, probably because of our historical development, of the Northwest Territories in the development of our political affairs.
The indemnity of our council members should be mentioned here, I believe, because it is much too low to attract the calibre of individual that you want to attract to this legislative body. The present members of the council are extremely idealistic people; if they were not they would not stay around long for the indemnity they get. Some of them are not going to run again simply because too much time is taken from their own businesses and the remuneration is really only nominal. I feel that the indemnity of council members should be increased.
The members of this committee will wonder why I am bringing this point to the minister's attention. The reason is simple. The members of the Yukon legislative council, as a body, cannot introduce or pass legislation which has anything to do with the expenditure of funds. This legislation must all be introduced by the commissioner, who is the personal representative of the minister in the Yukon Territory. The same situation prevails, I believe, in the Northwest Territories.
Supply-Northern Affairs
I want to mention, for want of a better or less inflammatory term, the bureaucratic rigidity of the administration in the Yukon. I do not make these remarks deprecatingly at all, but in the hope that I may get through to those in the administration who may read these remarks, and in the hope that the minister might devise some method of educating those who are responsible to him for the administrative functions of his department in the Yukon. I have no reason to suspect that the same conditions do not prevail in the administrative centres of the Northwest Territories. The bureaucratic rigidity of which I speak is a mental state more than anything else. It is a state in which all suggestions and ideas, unless they are those of the administration, are immediately received in a negative fashion. They are not received in such a way as to give the impression that the administration there wants new ideas. They are not fondled and developed if they are good or discarded if they are not good. These ideas are simply looked at with immediate prejudice and greeted with the remark, well, the department has this plan or that plan and anything less than that is not worthy of the consideration which obviously the person making the proposal has given to it.
I want to make it clear that I do not advance these remarks deprecatingly at all. However, there is a certain outlook toward these things by the administration which I feel has to be changed. If this rigidity continues it can only retard development. As a specific example in this regard I might cite the load limits in the Yukon Territory. The administration, without any real consideration of the matter, at one time imposed arbitrary limits on Yukon roads which affected the outflow of mining products from those areas. This was done without any study by the administration and, I believe to the credit of the minister's predecessor and his officials, without consultation with the department here. Nevertheless this is the type of thing-

I thank the committee for its courtesy. I should like to say also that such rigidity on the part of the administration discourages settlement in these northern areas. In this regard I would point specifically to the hundreds of applications for land in the Yukon. When an applicant decides he would

Supply-Northern Affairs like a piece of land upon which to settle, it sometimes takes years to get through all the red tape and obtain a lease. There are cases in which it has taken as long as six or seven years from the date on which the applicant applied for a plot of land before he has been told he can have the land or he cannot.
I realize that the whole organization has been altered in respect of this matter and I must say that, having read the outline of the reorganization, I consider it to be a great advance over the previous procedures. Nevertheless some impetus must still be given to eliminate these undue and retarding factors that exist in the present policy. For instance, I am sure the minister is aware of the fact that a price of $16 per acre has been set on agricultural land. Here in Ontario this might seem to be a meagre amount for an acre of agricultural land. However, in the north, where growing is a problem anyway, I am given to understand this amount is about five times greater than the same acre of land would cost in northern Alberta or northern British Columbia. Agricultural development will not be achieved when the price of land is completely out of reach of the settlers who are going into this high cost area in an attempt to farm.
The salary and position of the commissioner, I think, should come under the scrutiny of the department. You cannot expect the commissioner of the Yukon Territory, whoever he might be, to accept the responsabilities involved in handling millions and millions of dollars on a salary of $13,000 per year. This position calls for a highly skilled excutive, and the salary should be commensurate with that position and should be such that we can attract the most capable men in industry to undertake the position of chief administrator. Certainly he should be at least at the deputy minister level.
The ordinances that are passed by the Yukon legislative council are all prepared here in Ottawa. This is an absolutely unacceptable process to have the ordinances prepared 4,000 miles from the seat of the local legislature. There is only one solution to that problem, and that is the creation of the position of law clerk for the Yukon legislative council. I believe that if the department looked hard enough and set an attractive enough salary, they would have no difficulty in getting a capable man to fill the position.
There is one other thing in connection with the political development of the north that I should like to mention. Under existing procedures the commissioner alone has the complete management of the territorial civil service, which is fairly considerable. The territory is partly administered by the federal

civil service, under the minister's department, and partly by the territorial civil service. This whole system of the territorial civil service should come under the closest scrutiny. Certainly it should not be under the management of one man, because the system is subject to abuse if this continues to be the case. I am not suggesting that there has been any abuse, but all members can immediately see the possibility of playing favourites by hiring friends and the possibility of taking out vindictiveness by firing enemies. The complete absence of any cohesive civil service organization in the territories simply means a denial of the fair application of those principles which we all like to think exist under the civil service commission of Canada. I feel that some miniature civil service commission is required in the Yukon so that we can develop procedures of a competitive nature and put job opportunities in the territorial civil service on a fair basis.
Another reason for a change in this situation is that there are no grievance procedures at all for employees of the territorial civil service. If the commissioner does not feel that he wants to accept the representations of an employee who feels himself to be aggrieved, he is not obliged to do so. There is no recourse for the employees whatsoever.
I have now concluded my remarks concerning the political development of the territory. I have other remarks to make on the material development and on the human development in the north. However, I feel that I should at this stage allow other members of the committee to rise. I will bring these other matters up for consideration at a later stage in these proceedings.

speechtext:
Before I come to the questions which I wish to bring before the minister I want to say a word in reply to what has been said by the hon. member for Yukon, who has just taken his seat. From time to time we see in the papers reports about the slow progress being made in the House of Commons, and every so often the leader of the house will tell us that we have spent so many days on this item and so many days on that subject. I wish to put on record here the statement that if we are going to play politics with every question that comes before the House of Commons, that situation can be the only result. If the government or members of the government party introduce political notes, they must expect to have replies made to them. The hon. member for Yukon said that this party had derided the vision. I think he said that he had heard nothing but derision of the vision. I have not been aware of any derision of anything by members of this party, certainly of no derision of the vision.

But if there has been derision of anything it has been derision of the ballyhoo which this government has put forward with regard to the northern vision.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Your own leader lead you in it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: How could members of this party deride the vision? The vision did not originate with the Tory party or with the present Prime Minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is rot.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is not rot. The vision originated with the party that created this department; I refer to the department that is before us now. That is something that was done since I have come to this House of Commons, and that is not so very long ago. If there had been no vision there would have been no Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. The hon. member should not allow himself to get carried away with the idea that there was no vision until the Conservative party took office. We do our work in a quieter and more effective way, without all the publicity and the ballyhoo which amounts to words and nothing else. If the hon. member wishes to make invidious comparisons may I say that one cannot just do it on the basis of dollars and cents. We must take into consideration the circumstances that prevailed at the time the allocations were made and when this department was set up. It had to be organized. The groundwork had to be done and plans had to be laid. That was done. Progress was made, and I am glad to note that progress is continuing, but let hon. members opposite not think that the north did not exist until they took office.

speechtext: Nobody would have known it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think the hon. member would wish to be fair. I gave to the previous administration large gobs of credit-more than I think it was warranted-in connection with planning.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He was not listening.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The people who live in the north are Canadians, as are the people who live in other parts of Canada, and they have every right to be provided with the public facilities and social amenities that are enjoyed by other Canadian citizens. In so far as industrial exploration is going on, that too is all to the good. But when it comes to industrial development of the north, my hon. friend should know that the north suffers from the same handicaps from which we suffer in the maritimes. One of those handicaps is the high cost of living. The cost of living must be high because we are so far away
Supply-Northern Affairs from distribution centres. Because we are far away from distribution centres we are also far away from markets.
If the industrial development of the north is going to be done by private enterprise, my hon. friend must know that nearness to markets will be one of the most important factors that will be taken into consideration. As long as a product can be manufactured in a locality where it can be done more cheaply and with lower transportation costs, and therefore can be marketed at a cheaper price, these developments are going to take precedence over development of the north. That is just pure economic realism. That is the difference between the party which I represent and the government supporters. We wish to be realistic about the matter. We do not wish to create any great fantasies in people's minds. We wish to tell them the plain facts and let them use their own common sense.
I wish to congratulate the minister on his promotion to the treasury benches. I also wish to compliment him on the way he has introduced his estimates. The minister's department does not touch my constituency very closely. In my riding we have a few Indians, but they are fully integrated and are not in receipt of any special benefits from any government department. I think the service from which my riding derives the most benefit is the roads to resources program. I wish to commend the government for instituting that program. It has been extremely beneficial to my province and to my own riding. I hope that program will be continued and extended.
Historic sites come under the minister's department. I should like to remind him that since we have had nearly 500 years of history, we have more historic sites in my province than there are in any other single province. I should like to see these historic sites preserved. At one time the French were in possession of my province and there was a French capital. There are many old sites such as the headquarters of the various people who came out with charters to colonize the country. In all these places there are sites which should be preserved.
In my own riding there is an old lighthouse which has been dismantled and which I think perhaps is doomed to fall down or be taken down unless something is done about it. Personally I should like to appeal to the minister to have this lighthouse preserved. It is not only a relic of an old structure; it is also a famous landmark. A diagram of it was printed on all the mariners' charts right up to the time of confederation. Whether that has been done since confederation I am not in a position to say. However, it is an historic

Supply-Northern Affairs site. It is located at Rose Blanche in my riding. It is a very famous landmark, easily recognized from the sea, and a great help to mariners in identifying their landfalls. It has a double purpose. In that respect it is utilitarian, as well as historic. I hope the minister will look into this matter and do something to enable this old structure to be preserved.
My main reason for rising today is to bring to the minister's attention the situation with regard to seals and whales. We commonly refer to a seal fishery and a whale fishery, but as everybody knows they are animals and not fish. Therefore I presume they come under the minister's department.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think I should point out to the hon. member that they actually come under the Department of Fisheries. Even though they may be classified as animals and mammals, they are dealt with by the Department of Fisheries.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I thank the minister for that information. The reason I raise this point now is that, I suppose quite wrongly, I was under the impression that a few days ago the minister replied to a question put by the hon. member for Kootenay West, or an hon. member on this side of the house, about the seal fishery. I thought the minister replied to that question and I inferred that these matters came under his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext: At that time I referred the question to the Minister of Fisheries, who has since dealt with the matter in the house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Thank you very much. In that case I will reserve my remarks on this subject until we come to the proper item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks at this time will be associated in the main with the tourist industry aspect of the department. In this regard may I join the many hon. members who have spoken previously in praise of the efficiency of the Canadian travel bureau and the energetic head of this bureau, Mr. Alan Field.
I should like to quote a few passages from the annual proceedings of the Canadian tourist association at its convention of 1960. In this publication the association brings to everyone's attention the fact that Canada is still showing a deficit in our tourist trade with our neighbour to the south. The association also points to the fact that this deficit continues to be quite substantial and that every effort must be made to reduce this deficit as much as possible. On page 2 of the convention proceedings the association points out that travel expenditures by United States citizens outside the United States have increased by more than 300 per cent in the


past decade, and that Canada has unfortunately been able to attract only 23 per cent of this business.
After having attended meetings of the mines, forests and waters committee for two years, before which officials of the Canadian tourist association and others interested in the tourist industry in Canada have appeared, I know that a great many things have been accomplished by this government in an effort to attract greater numbers of United States citizens to Canada. One particular accomplishment was the erecting of a sign, "Great White Way", in New York City last summer. I would appreciate hearing the minister's comments on what the government feels has been accomplished through this unique effort in endeavouring to attract tourists from that area to Canada.
The Atlantic area is tremendously interested in new ways and means of attracting tourists to Canada, and especially to our particular area. The tourist industry is big business in the maritimes, and I feel it is one area where we can give leadership, and have already given leadership, to the rest of Canada in our methods of attracting tourists. In this regard the Atlantic provinces tourist bureaux have worked very closely with the Canadian travel bureau, and I feel they have accomplished a great deal in this matter of attracting tourists. I feel that tourist accommodation facilities in the Atlantic area are second to none in Canada. I am quite certain that the tremendous number of repeat visits by tourists is an indication of the high class accommodation that is available to them in this area. In my province of Nova Scotia this has, in part at least, been the result of the very progressive program initiated by the provincial government in assisting tourist operators to provide the necessary plant and accommodation facilities for those who visit our area.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
At one o'clock I was bringing to the attention of the committee the very progressive nature of the legislation which has been made available to the tourist industry in Nova Scotia and showing how this legislation had assisted to a large extent in making Nova Scotia one of the leaders in Canada in the type of accommodations which are available to tourists. This does not mean that Nova Scotia is satisfied that the accommodations available are the best that can

be made available. Indeed, in the field of restaurant operations there is still much that can be done and I am sure all restaurant operators not only in Nova Scotia but throughout Canada will be very pleased with the provisions of the Small Business Loans Act and the benefits which will accrue to them as a result of the facilities provided by this act.
Earlier in this debate we heard the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo express his opinion of the action which this government has taken through the department of northern affairs. In effect, the hon. member said we were doing no more than was done by the former Liberal administration. My own opinion is that many people in Canada will find a great many holes to pick in that argument. Certainly in my own province the roads to resources program put into effect by this administration has proved a boon to the provincial government in providing highway facilities in areas which otherwise would not be able to receive those benefits.
To bring matters closer to home, in my own constituency of Cumberland the roads to resources program has been of great assistance to the provincial government in the construction of two highways. One of them, known as the Tidnish shore road, is just about complete at the present time and makes available to tourists some 20 miles of the most beautiful salt water beaches in Canada. When completed this highway will cost approximately $1,100,000 half of which will be paid by this government through the department of northern affairs. To say that this is no more than was done prior to 1957 is just being unrealistic and such a statement is not justified by the facts.
This is not the only important road in my constituency. There is another highway known as the Parrsboro shore road. As a result of the roads to resources program the provincial government has been able to undertake the reconstruction of this road and its eventual paving at an estimated cost of close to $600,000. This will be of tremendous benefit to the people of the town of Parrsboro and to those who live along the Parrsboro shore. This is an outstanding piece of highway from a scenic point of view. It has been called by many in our area the little Cabot trail because the type of scenery along this shore line is very similar to that found in Cape Breton. No doubt, when this road is completed, there will be a tremendous influx of tourists into the region. These are tourists who apparently would never be as willing to travel along this beautiful highway from Diligent River, to Port Gerville to Ward's Brook, to Advocate Harbour and Apple River, if it were not for the fact that it were paved. This
Supply-Northern Affairs represents the type of thinking, now prevalent in this department, which results in tremendous benefits to every individual in Canada.
Along the same line, we could consider park sites and picnic and camping grounds which are now available to tourists of the type that, until this government put into effect this type of legislation, could not come to Canada because of the lack of money necessary for accommodation in motels or hotels. The popularity of this legislation is indicated by the tremendous use being made of these facilities. We still do not have enough of this type of facility, but one should consider how few we would have if we had gone along as the former Liberal administration did until 1957. Certainly the provinces could not have done this on their own or, if they had, could not have done it to the same extent. In my own constituency, as in other constituencies in Nova Scotia and the rest of Canada, there are a greater number of facilities available which attract tourists and perhaps induce them to stay longer. In this respect the government should be complimented highly for its progressive thinking.
There is in my opinion the need for a second national park on the mainland of Nova Scotia. Cape Breton has probably as beautiful a park as exists in the Dominion of Canada. It is a park with tremendous facilities, in respect of which this government has done a tremendous amount of work. This park attracts and is attracting a great number of tourists who come to Nova Scotia. It is my feeling, however, that mainland Nova Scotia has areas which would be very attractive to tourists. Certainly I would not want to prevent anyone from going to Cape Breton and witnessing the grandeur of the Margaree valley and the Cabot Trail. These places are beautiful beyond compare. I feel everyone who goes to Nova Scotia should certainly make an effort to visit Cape Breton to take in the scenic wonders. However, I do feel that there is room for another national park in Nova Scotia and would suggest that there is an area in my own constituency which would lend itself to this type of development. I would suggest the department give consideration to the establishment of such a park in the Wentworth-Westchester area of Cumberland. This area has many of the features one would look for in the establishment of a national park, and I would recommend it to the minister for consideration.
I might point out that there have been camp sites and picnic grounds established there during the past year which have been of tremendous value to tourists, for which the federal government can assume at least part of the credit. There was a very fine motel

Supply-Northern Affairs
established there recently. It was built partially through assistance under the legislation made available under the Stanfield government. In this area we have the very finest skiing accommodation available in Nova Scotia. The eastern part of Canada has a very short summer tourist season and I feel consideration should be given to the possibility of developing tourist attractions during the winter months. I feel that the Wentworth skiing area should be enlarged. If this area were made part of a national park this could be done with a good deal of benefit resulting to everyone in Nova Scotia who is interested in skiing. Since the government has indicated its interest in the physical fitness of our people, I would suggest that there is no better way of providing outdoor recreational facilities than by developing skiing areas.
I would point out that in Nova Scotia, as in many areas in Canada, particularly the smaller communities, no facilities exist for our younger and older citizens to partake in outdoor physical fitness programs except, perhaps, in hunting, fishing and hiking. It may be that the government in considering the different proposals put forward will be willing to give consideration to the establishment of an act under which moneys could be made available to these areas to assist in the construction of recreational centres.
In my home town of Amherst there exists an armoury and a beautiful new arena. In these two buildings there is room for many recreational activities. Many towns in my constituency have neither an armoury nor an arena and, if we could assist these communities in the construction of some sort of auditorium where recreational activities could be carried out, it would be of great benefit to the physical fitness of our citizens.
I would like to add at this time that the citizens of Nova Scotia have benefited from the programs of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources since 1957. Prior to that time I am sure many citizens were hardly even aware that such a department was in existence. As a result of the establishment of the roads to resources program and the camping ground-picnic site program we have witnessed a tremendous difference in the interest and feeling of our citizens toward this department. I am sure that the present minister, as the former minister, will do everything he possibly can to assist those areas of Canada in taking advantage of their national resources.
Last evening the hon. member for Port Arthur made some comments about the minister to the effect that he was disappointed, and that the minister had been long enough in this position to indicate how aggressive he was and where he was going to take this

department. Usually the hon. member for Port Arthur is fairly responsible when speaking in this house, but on this particular occasion I would say that he allowed his tongue to carry him somewhat away in expressing his regrets over the ability of the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
I think it would be very irresponsible of the minister were he, after a few months, to start making grandiose statements about what he is going to do as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I think he is being most responsible in assessing what can be done, how best it can be done, and doing so in a workmanlike manner. I think the hon. member for Port Arthur will find that it would be difficult indeed to find a more aggressive individual than the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Let us give him a little time to prove this and not knock him before he has had a real chance to prove his ability. Thank you very much.
