I have started off by stirring up some people and I must say the chamber is somewhat more alert now than it was a few minutes ago; therefore I have accomplished something in that respect. But I do wiant to say a few words on these very important estimates. They range over a very wide field and affect the lives of a large number of Canadians who live in a way different from that of the majority of us. The administration required in the area which concerns most of those people is somewhat different from the normal administration of a department, and I am quite sure it tests the ability of the administrators because of the different circumstances and the different conditions under which some sections of this department operate.
I suppose it is only fitting and proper that I should congratulate the minister on his appointment, although I do so with a degree

of envy because I have been in the British Columbia legislature and this house for 20 years. I am just as close to becoming a cabinet minister now as I was when I started.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am very glad I have some agreement on one point, anyway.
I think everyone realizes that the minister comes from a family with an excellent record of public service in the district in which he lives. He has distinguished academic achievements and his record of public service in the welfare council and the Legion and as a university teacher is well known. He had a very distinguished and courageous record during the war period, which we all recognize. Some people think the minister is modest but, you know, he is well able to blow his own horn because I have stood on the street corner and heard him do it. In the very best sense of the word, he is a good musician and I hope he plays in the orchestra of parliament to some public advantage in the days ahead. For some 10 years the minister was a conscientious and industrious private member of this house. With his appointment as minister in charge of this department he faces the test as to his ability as an administrator and, we trust, a creator in so far as policy is concerned and as an innovator because I think a person with these qualities is required in a department of this kind. We hope the minister accepts the challenge that his present position offers him and as the years go by demonstrates his continuing courage in facing new and difficult situations and his understanding of the requirements of the moment.
I wish to make a few comments. Does the member wish to say something?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We are still waiting for the hon. member to say something.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I shall get to the point. We shall take full advantage of the estimates of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to let him realize that his estimates are of great importance in this house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Try to deal with these, first.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I shall want to get his views on the export of power in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We should like to get the hon. member's.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
They have already been stated publicly. I want to say a word or two about the resources for tomorrow conference, which we all support and of which we are very glad to see this minister in charge. We are happy that he has found time to promote it. However, I do want to complement the remarks made by the hon. member for Port
Supply-Northern Affairs Arthur by saying that every opportunity should be given to all sections of the community to make a contribution to this conference by invitation, and this includes labour and some other sections of the community that have not been invited to date. I know it may appear that a conference such as this may become, shall I say, too cumbersome and top-heavy, but I think every opportunity should be given for wide spread participation and women's organizations should be given an invitation to attend this conference if only as observers because it is a conference that will decide matters of importance to the country as a whole.
I wish to say a word or two about the travel bureau and our tourist industry. Recently I read an article in a paper entitled "Canada's Ailing Tourist Industry; Can It Be Cured?" I think we all agree that during recent years the tourist industry has been somewhat of a disappointment; that Canadians have been spending more abroad, particularly since 1957, than United States tourists and others have been spending in Canada. I am not going to blame the government entirely for that; it is a reflection of economic conditions in the United States as well as here, but I do suggest that some serious consideration will have to be given to this subject and to increasing, shall I say, the tempo of Canadian appeal abroad. I noticed recently that Premier Bennett provided a haven for one of his former ministers, the former minister of agriculture, as tourist publicity representative in San Francisco. He was a very successful salesman of Carnation milk prior to being minister, and I hope he is just as successful in selling British Columbia as a place for tourists to visit. In this connection, I simply want to conclude my remarks on this point by suggesting that the Kootenays are often overlooked in the advertising which the minister's department directs to tourists. Mention is made of the coastal areas and the Okanagan, but I think the minister will find I am correct when I say there is much less reference to the beauties of the Kootenays. I should like him to take action to correct this situation because my constituents who are interested in the tourist industry have made this complaint for a number of years.
While I am on my feet, I should like to say a word or two about the historic sites and monuments board. The hon. member who spoke before me made a reference to it, and I intended to make a reference to the subject when the particular item was under discussion. However, I might as well do so now. I am sure the minister is interested in assisting in the preservation of historic sites

Supply-Northern Affairs and monuments that are worth while and to which the federal government can properly make a contribution.
I want to bring to the attention of the committee the excellent work that has been done by the Kootenay historical society in the preservation of the steamship Moyie at Kaslo, B.C. This is the last of the stern-wheelers that have plied the lakes of the interior since 1884. The residents of Kaslo have gone out of their way to do what they could to bring this vessel ashore, place it on a foundation and make a museum out of its interior. Their efforts have been rewarded by an increasing number of tourists who want to see one of these vessels that sailed the lakes for so many years. The residents of this area have received assitance from the federal government, and quite recently they applied for some further assistance. I merely mention this in the hope the minister will give further consideration to their pleas for the further assistance necessary in completing the preservation of this vessel and its caretaking in the future.
I should like now to say a few words with respect to the concern of the rod and gun clubs of the interior over the possible developments on the Columbia and the effect of these dams on fishing in the area. This has been a subject of considerable discussion. Quite recently I might say all the rod and gun clubs of the interior met at a conference in Vernon. These clubs represent 3,200 members and they unanimously expressed their opposition to the building of the high Arrow dam. They have also given very careful consideration to the effect of these dams, should they be constructed, upon the fish and wildlife of the area.
This resolution was adopted by the West Kootenay rod and gun clubs association, by the interior rod and gun clubs association and by the B.C. rod and gun clubs association. I read it because these men have had a number of committees working which, with the co-operation of the game branch of British Columbia, have been studying the impact of this flooding upon wildlife and fishing. This is the resolution:
Whereas the impact on wildlife of Kootenay river and Columbia river development of power and storage dams will be tremendous and the adequate correction of the problems created will be much beyond the financial ability of the fish and game branch of the department of recreation and conservation of the government of British Columbia,
Therefore be it resolved (1) that a complete and detailed biological survey be carried out jointly by the Canadian wildlife service and the fish and game branch, B. C. department of recreation and conservation, to determine the ecological effect on wildlife of each and all proposed power and storage dams, the report of such survey to be publicly available; (2) that anticipated problems in wildlife management as indicated in the

survey be planned for, rectified, and financed as part of said developments; (3) that a definite proportion of the value of the power produced be set aside and other benefits such as navigation, irrigation, etc. (including downstream benefits) produced from said developments for wildlife management and recreational facilities in the Kootenay and Columbia river basins in Canada.
We realize that this study cannot be undertaken without co-operation between federal and provincial agencies. I do urge the minister to give consideration to this problem because it is of great concern to a large number of persons interested in preserving wildlife and fish in the southeastern portion of British Columbia.
I should like to refer briefly to an answer the minister gave in reply to one of my questions some days ago with regard to the Arctic islands. I had mentioned that Commander Low planted the flag on Ellesmere island and took possession of that island and the islands of the north in the name of the Dominion of Canada. The minister indicated that my knowledge of history was somewhat inaccurate and that this taking possession had somehow been accomplished before. In order to refresh the minister's memory, I should like to read to him the terms of reference given to Commander Low:
The expedition had three objectives:
(1)	to establish the Royal Northwest Mounted Police (R.C.M.P.) as the law and order agency in the eastern Arctic;
(2)	to take formal possession of all the Arctic islands in the name of King Edward VII and the Dominion of Canada;
(3)	to gather information on the health of the Eskimos, the geology, botany and other resources, and produce topographical surveys of the areas visited.
Then, there are more detailed instructions given. However, according to my reading of Canadian history and a searching of the record, I find that is the first occasion on which, under instructions of the federal government, the commander or an expedition took formal possession of all the Arctic islands in the name of Canada. If I am wrong I wish the minister would let the committee have the source of his information because, in a very moderate manner, he corrected my statement the other day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Will the hon. member indicate the document from which he is reading?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, it is an extract from the book "The Neptune" which was written in connection with the voyage of the Neptune.
I should like to refer to another matter. In Hansard of July 6, 1956, page 5691, I outlined the part Dr. L. E. Borden, who is a personal friend of mine now resident in Victoria and a relative of the late Sir Robert

Borden, had played in establishing our claim to the Arctic islands. Then, on August 11, 1956, I had the honour, on Dr. Borden's behalf, of presenting to the house an original proclamation taking possession of Ellesmere land and all the adjacent islands. This important document is now in the archives bound in red leather, if any of the newcomers to the house wish to see evidence of this proclamation, they will find it there.
Mrs. Borden wrote an article in the Canadian Geographical Journal entitled "Northward 1903-04". Since this article appeared a further development of the utmost importance has occurred. I am sure hon. members are all aware of the contribution that Vilhjalmur Stefansson, consultant, polar studies program at Dartmouth college, Hanover, New Hampshire, has made in relation to scientific work in the polar regions. Upon reading Mrs. Borden's article, he wrote her the first thing next morning because of his book "Cancer, Disease of Civilization?" published in 1960. I quote:
This was the first cancer search among the northern Canadian Eskimo ever formally directed by the Canadian (or any North American) government.
He has written to mention this matter because at the time and since then Dr. Borden never received credit for undertaking the first cancer research with respect to the Eskimos and making a report on that research to the government of Canada, which research has been confirmed by the later experience of the department of national health and this government. In fairness to this unusual work done by Dr. Borden at that time I want to quote briefly from two letters from Dr. Stefansson. He writes as follows to Mrs. Borden on February 5, 1961:
Your letter of 31 January is both a relief and depressing. When I read your "Northward 1903-04" I had a sinking feeling that I had failed to give due credit to Dr. Borden for an Eskimo cancer search on the Neptune and now I am, though absolved of personal guilt by your letter, nevertheless depressed by the story which is sad news that accidentally, through parsimony, or deliberately, his scientific work, and that of others, was lost or suppressed. If published with the rest of the Neptune report in 1906 then Dr. Borden, Commander Low, and the Canadian government might have had the credit for an important pioneer research on the incidence of cancer-and I am sure his cancer report, which your letter summarizes, cannot have been the only notable thing that would have been established by the publication of his findings.
Then he goes on to say this:
Monday I shall be sending to you an inscribed copy of "Cancer: Disease of Civilization?" You will find that in this title the "?" is meant to be conspicuous, and you will see how consonant Dr. Borden's findings are with the rest of the Eskimo testimonies, all the way from southwestern Alaska to southeastern and northeastern Canada, and how well Dr. Borden deserves to have his name at the head of the list-if only I had known enough to place it there!
90205-6-246
Supply-Northern Affairs
The letter is signed by Dr. Stefansson. 1 make this reference because I think it is only fair. As I said on July 6, 1956, the accomplishments of this expedition have largely been buried, lost sight of and forgotten. Here I have further evidence of the good work undertaken by this expedition, first of all in claiming the Arctic islands on behalf of Canada, second in surveys and third in botanical research. Dr. Borden produced the first botanical survey of the Arctic islands. Now we have proof that he was the first one to write a report on cancer research with respect to the Eskimos on the North American continent.
I bring this matter to the minister's attention because I think it is only fitting and proper that a gentleman of these accomplishments, who is still living in Victoria, should be recognized and his work brought to the attention of the House of Commons and the country.

Mr. Chairman, I wish that the minister would suggest to the historic sites and monuments board of Canada that they put up a monument on the grounds of the College de l'Assomption, or a memorial plaque on the century-old part of the building, in memory of Sir Wilfrid Laurier who was a student there.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier was of the 22nd promotion. He entered the college in 1854 and left it in 1860.
Founded in 1833 by the Rev. Frangois Labelle, parish priest, and by doctors J. B. Meilleur and J. C. Cazeneuve, the College de l'Assomption has given the church and the state many prominent figures, such as Sir Wilfrid Laurier, one of its most renowned former pupils, Sir Louis-Amable Jette, lieutenant-governor, and, among members of the clergy-let me mention only a few-Msgr. Charlebois, Msgr. Lamarche and the present superior, Msgr. Langlois, P.D.
May I quote from the records of the College de l'Assomption, in which I find the following:
After the general election of 1900,... the superior of the college sent a telegram of congratulations to Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Obviously the latter was very pleased and he answered without delay-
I have here a photostat of the letter he wrote:
Ottawa, November 10th, 1900
Dear Mr. Villeneuve,
Among all the congratulations I have received on the results of the general election, none pleased me more than the ones coming from my alma mater. I am always proud of having been a student at the College de l'Assomption.
Yours truly,
Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

Supply*-Northern Affairs
I feel therefore that a monument, or else a plaque affixed to the hundred-year old section of the College de l'Assomption would remind the people of L'Assomption, and the country as a whole, that Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier was educated at that college.
I express that request with the conviction that it will be taken into serious consideration by the historic sites and monuments board of Canada.
I wish now to refer to a series of questions which I put to the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources concerning Eskimo school children of northern Quebec and of other areas in the north. He answered among other things:
-English is the language of instruction in the schools established by the department of northern affairs for Eskimos generally. This has been the practice in northern Quebec as well as the Northwest Territories since the first departmental school was established in 1949.
Mr. Chairman, may I add that that situation was created and has existed since 1949, in other words, under the Liberal administration of which the member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), as minister of transport, was a member, as was the present premier of Quebec Mr. Jean Lesage, as minister of northern affairs and national resources and who was therefore chiefly responsible for that situation. I wanted to remind the house that such was the kind of vision he had at that time.
Those are the only comments I had to make. (Text):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As a member from one of the great northern territories-in as much as my district includes Labrador, it is needless to say that I am greatly interested in the estimates of this department. I should like to begin by congratulating the minister on his appointment. As time goes on I trust that he will not forget the vision because, as I have said before in this chamber, far from deriding the vision I agree wholeheartedly with the scriptures where it is written, "Where there is no vision the people perish". As a matter of fact, the record of history shows htat almost every great endeavour could never have been carried through to fruition without vision and the courage and faith which must accompany it. When any new thing is started it must be done, by virtue of its newness, with inadequate knowledge and insufficient evidence. Vision therefore is of tremendous importance.
Northern development is important to Canada. Vast as is our territory, our population basically is strung out on a ribbon along the southern border. If we are to develop

into the really great and powerful nation which we can and which I am sure we will become, it is necessary to keep northern development always to the fore.
With regard to the authorship of the vision,
I agree with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, who pointed out that northern development had its roots in the previous Liberal administration. In so far as the vision which began some years ago is carried on and augmented, it must receive our support.
Perhaps I may be forgiven if I again refer to holy writ with respect to the youthfulness of the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I think of a text which in my mind couples him with the hon. member for Kootenay West. The text is, "Your young men shall see visions and your old men shall dream dreams".
My criticism of the vision is that it has not been broad enough. The vision of the present administration has been too narrow in its beam. It has been a northwest vision, rather than a really broad northern vision.
I make of the new minister the request which I made of his predecessor, that he beam northern development broader so as to include Labrador to a greater extent. Nowadays Labrador is very much in the news and I need not remind hon. members of the vast developments which are taking place there at Carol lake, lake Wabush, the Twin Falls power development, and so on. However, these developments are largely a result of provincial vision and the foresightedness of Premier Smallwood.
Labrador is a great part of the north and its wealth is now beginning to be recognized. I would ask the minister to take into serious consideration the possibility of building federal roads and airstrips in that great territory, which eventually will be recognized as a veritable treasure house of Canada. Before it can properly be developed and before its tremendous potential in respect to the tourist industry can be developed, a number of airstrips and roads must be built. We must build a road around the coast and a road linking the interior with the north shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence.
With respect to the Eskimos who live in Labrador, as hon. members know Eskimo affairs in Labrador are administered by the provincial government with assistance from the federal government.
I should like to request that the federal government give the same per capita assistance to Labrador Eskimos as it gives to Quebec Eskimos. According to figures tabled in the house, the Quebec Eskimo receives federal assistance to the extent of $400 per person. I think that when the sum total of federal

assistance to the Eskimo in Labrador is taken into account it will be found that he receives much less; perhaps less than $250 per person.
This is something to which I ask the minister to give very sympathetic attention and, if possible, as soon as practicable make available to the government of Newfoundland financial assistance for the Eskimos of Labrador to the same degree as that assistance is made available to the Eskimos of Quebec.
I hope, of course, that Indians will receive the same treatment as Eskimos. While on the subject of Eskimos I should like to pay a tribute to the missionaries of all faiths who are carrying on great work amongst the Eskimos and Indians of Labrador. Their dedication, self-sacrifice and invaluable work in connection with these people is very great indeed. There is really no way of measuring its great worth.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister something which I mentioned last year. I refer to the desirability of having a monument erected to the last of the Beothics, the original inhabitants of Newfoundland. The last Beothic was Mary March, and I believe her place of burial is known. It occurred to me that perhaps we could erect a monument in the Terra Nova national park to the last of that tragic race. I think that would be appropriate. It would be a token of remembrance to a race of original Canadians which has completely disappeared.
There is another matter which has been brought to my attention by my constituents in Gander, the desirability of a golf course in the Terra Nova national park. The Terra Nova national park is in the constituency of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. His riding and mine are adjoining. The people of Gander are very interested in a golf course for the Terra Nova national park. Perhaps it is not quite fair for me to ask for a golf course in the Terra Nova national park especially for the benefit of my constituents in Gander, but I think a golf course in the Terra Nova national park would be a considerable attraction to tourists. I hope the minister will keep this in mind.
I would also ask the minister to keep in mind the question of the road to Eastport through the national park. I think a survey was carried out in connection with this road. I hope the survey will be completed in time for the road to be built perhaps late this year as a part of a winter works program. This road is used extensively by my constituents as well as those of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Another matter I should like to mention is the general encouragement of tourists to visit Newfoundland and Labrador and the 90205-6-246J
Supply-Northern Affairs possibility of extending existing steamship services and adapting one of them for the use of tourists in Labrador.
Labrador is a great and unknown territory. I am justly proud of it and I think more people should have the opportunity of seeing it. Gander itself is a logical place for a centre of tourism, and a ski-run would probably encourage tourists to come to central Newfoundland and would make it more attractive to them.
To return for a moment to the question of Labrador, as I said earlier it is not only a treasure house of the north, or a treasure house of the province of Newfoundland, but it is a treasure house of Canada. I should like to repeat that there is a great need for opening up this vast territory, which to some extent is one of the last unknown and unspoiled areas in the world. Certainly it is to the advantage of Canada as a nation to have Labrador opened up by road and air through the building of airstrips. I think this work should be begun as quickly as possible, particularly the building of airstrips, followed by the building of federal roads.
I am sure it would be a sound investment and an investment which would pay off literally in dollars and cents over the years. It would be a great Canadian project which would be good for Canada as well as for Labrador. I hope the minister will consider this, though it is admittedly a big item, in the light of what northern development really is, a huge undertaking challenging the imagination and requiring courageous action.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It is always a great privilege to stand in this chamber and speak a few words, but this is particularly the case when we are able to congratulate a new and young minister. We in the party perhaps know better than most, the hon. gentleman who now holds office as Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and we have every hope that he will bring new lustre to the vision. Far from the vision not being broad enough I am sure it is only a matter of getting enough appropriation to carry out the plan which he and his ministry have in mind for the development of the north country.
I also represent a great frontier constituency in northwestern Alberta and our main problem up there is transportation. Perhaps unfortunately, our whole district is within the provincial boundaries and for this reason neither the new minister nor his department can take the initiative in providing roads to resources. This is probably not too well understood, but I want to put it on record because it is the case; it is only where a province makes overtures to the dominion government that we are able to assist them in building roads in

Supply-Northern Affairs the province. The district of which I am speaking is some 60,000 square miles in extent and in the northern half roads are almost non-existent. Transportation is essential to any orderly development of the north country. The most important object of building a good road is, of course, to reduce freight rates into the north country. Without such reduction the rate of development is bound to slow down. I know that every co-operation will be given when the provincial authorities seek to put in a road, preferably an allweather road, to serve the district surrounding McMurray.
The resources in the north have not been touched. In my opinion there are several parts of this region which should be opened up, areas closer than the far reaches of the Canadian shield. I refer to Wood Buffalo park and the Thelon game reserve. At present we are unable to prospect for minerals in that part of the country. It may have been in order at one time to restrict prospecting for minerals in the parks but I think that is unnecessary in Wood Buffalo park. It is a very extensive area and the usual reasons for not prospecting-interference with the beauty of the park or with wildlife-do not apply in this case because the 15,000 or 20,000 buffalo that have their habitat in this park do not live in the area where the prospecting would be done.
We have opened up the park for the clearance of timber. This was instituted under the former administration and I do not intend to go into that question at the present time, but I must say I was not happy at all about the methods used to take this timber out. I understand the timber is over aged. If it can be taken out for the good of the economy and for the good of the park, I see no reason why the minerals should not be prospected for and removed as long as this does not interfere with the natural beauty of the park or the safety and security of the animals.
The Clearwater river area is also very rich in natural resources especially those likely to prove of benefit to the tourist industry. Some of the finest big game hunting in the world can be found in there; some of the finest tro-phys, the antlers from elk, moose and deer, have come out of the Clearwater river area. But, again, we cannot go into this area without a proper road. I cannot sufficiently emphasize the necessity of pressing for a suitable all-weather road into the McMurray area and I look to this ministry to give every cooperation to the provincial authorities when they are ready to take this initiative.
I should like to congratulate the department for assisting in providing picnic shelters along the various roads of Canada. Wherever you go you see these fine facilities. I do not think the part which the federal government has

played in providing the shelters is sufficiently well known and I want to take this opportunity to express my personal thanks. I have used them often myself, and I know they are much appreciated.
I think a larger appropriation should be granted in respect of our national parks so that more employment might be provided for our high school and university students, these fine young boys and girls who are seeking to continue their education and improve their capacities. These young people are going to provide the most valuable natural resource we have in this whole Dominion of Canada and I should like to see a much larger appropriation made in respect of our national parks to provide jobs for as many of them as we possibly can.
I should also like to ask the minister if he can explain the reason for having the R.C.M.P. member dropped from the Northwest Territories Council. As an ex-member of the force I can speak with some knowledge of this matter. It may be misunderstood throughout the ranks of the serving members of the force why a senior officer should not sit on this council, because the prestige of the force, as every Canadian knows, is of paramount importance in the north country. I should like it to be made as clear as possible why this official is no longer required or needed on this council. This is a personal matter and not intended as criticism but as a personal observation.
May I say I would not be in favour of the withdrawal of mounted police detachments from outlying posts in the north country. I know that every young member of the mounted police wishes at one time or another to serve in the north. He wants to be on detachment duty. He wants to have the responsibility for getting to know the natives and of establishing that very special and responsible relationship with the natives which has been traditionally part of R.C.M.P. fife and work in those areas in the past. If there is any thought of bringing in outlying detachments and centralizing them in any southern posts, it is my opinion that it will not work. It will not work as far as the morale of the mounted police is concerned and I do not think it will work as far as the natives themselves are concerned. It takes years to get to know these people and you cannot get to know them sitting in Fort Smith or Frobisher Bay. One must mingle with the natives and understand their thinking to be of any use at all to them in standing between the native's way of life and the doubtful advantages of the white man's civilization.
The minister has just returned from the north country and I know that he will now

be in a much better position to make decisions in that regard. I think it is very dangerous for someone to sit in Ottawa and make decisions without going first into the Arctic to acquire an understanding of the situation there. I think very careful planning and consideration of the many human resources which exist in the north country must take place before this vision can be successful, as every Canadian hopes it will be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for Port Arthur is not yet dejected and sorry because of the harsh strictures which he passed with regard to the minister, possibly I can say a few more words which will cause him to understand the situation.
The northern affairs and national resources portfolio is a difficult one. With deference, it is my submission that it is not possible for any one man to place himself in possession of all the facts regarding the various projects which are normally attended to in this department, as well as the special projects, one of which was mentioned by the hon. member. I refer, of course, to the resources for tomorrow conference. I would suggest this is a department of government which is tremendously important and complex, and will require very considerable time and effort to master. I am sure the hon. member for Port Arthur will not mind my saying that sometimes we feel that his party considers that achievements are measured by the mileage of speeches, and success, by the amount of noise and confusion. I say quite sincerely to the hon. member that the present position to which his party has now descended is a good criterion that this is not the way to gain the esteem of the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont took it upon himself yesterday to deliver the usual strictures and jeers with regard to the northern development program of this government. I would suggest this stems from the attitude on the part of hon. members of the official opposition, and is recognition of their dismal failure to do those things they should have done which are so important to have been done at the proper time which was, I suggest, while that party was in office.
I have been living in the north for almost one third of a century. I include my own district of Peace River in the north. I do not believe that these developments will take place suddenly and with great rapidity but that we must establish a foundation and move from one position to another. This is precisely what the present government is doing. I have driven along the Mackenzie highway which, during the course of last year, was extended to Yellowknife, and have seen dozens of cars
Supply-Northern Affairs carrying tourists looking for a land of opportunity with the feeling that somewhere in the north there is that area where they can find themselves in a life different from that to which they have been accustomed. It is the bettering of the means of transportation that will lead to this particular achievement.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont tried to disparage this government's achievement while, at the same time, tried to horn in on those achievements by stating that they stemmed from the efforts of the previous government. In support of that contention he cited certain statements which had been made by Mr. Lesage when he was the minister of northern affairs and national resources. I have read the statements made by Mr. Lesage to a parliamentary committee in 1955, as set out by the hon. member, and have come to the conclusion that they are no more than a generalization of policy. It is like saying that one is against sin and believes in motherhood, only more so. At page 7 in the English translation of the speech made by the hon. member, in Hansard of yesterday, he quotes Mr. Lesage as follows:
Mr. Chairman, I have given an outline of our policy to cope with the human problem of economic development in the north. I do not believe our plans lack imagination, vigour or aggressiveness.
That statement may be so. All they lacked was action.	*
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont made some mention of the Great Slave lake railway project. I would like to deal with this subject in the time remaining at my disposal.
I recall a statement made by the hon. member for Laurier when he was speaking on the resolution for the establishment of the sessional committee on railways. At that time he queried the delay on the part of this government in initiating this plan to construct this railway, which had been announced in 1958 in the speech from the throne. He was suggesting that this government was slow in consummating this project. I suggest that any delay which may have taken place in the construction of this very essential, important and vital project can be laid squarely at the door of the previous government. I have had in my possession for some time information with regard to this particular project but have not made use of it for the simple reason that so long as the royal commission established by the government to inquire into this route was in operation the matter was sub judice.
This commission was set up under terms of reference dated some time in May or June of 1959. Its deliberations were completed, to the extent that a report was forthcoming, toward the end of last session, and

Supply-Northern Affairs consequently nothing could be done last year. This year when parliament reconvened there was contained in the speech from the throne a statement to the effect that a location survey would be made of the western route. I take that statement to indicate, as I feel most individuals will, that the government has accepted the majority recommendation of that royal commission and has decided on a western route for the construction of this railway. If I have enough time left I propose to give the reasons why this is a proper decision.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont made reference to a brief filed by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories with the Gordon royal commission. I read that brief and feel that it was well laid out, well buttressed by facts, statistics and information. As I read the brief, it was specifically and definitely in favour of the construction of this railroad in so far as it dealt with the establishment of a northern development program hinged on transportation. In regard to the construction of this railroad it contained recommendations that a route commencing at Grimshaw and going to Peace river should be adopted. So far as I can find out, up until two or three years ago, this is the only route that had been ever deemed acceptable.
In support of this I would refer to a document or a pamphlet-I think it is called "Canada's New North"-which was put out by the department of northern affairs in 1947, I believe, under the very capable direction of Dr. Camsell, who had a most adequate and informed knowledge of the northern situation. In this particular pamphlet reference was made to this question of the railroad to Great Slave lake. The report took cognizance of various suggestions which had been made in the past and then went on to say it repeated and accepted the fact that the only logical and proper route was the one from Grimshaw. This is the one going from the Peace river country, the western route. All others which had been considered with regard to this particular project had been found to be lacking in so far as the principles of economics and engineering are concerned. Therefore, so far as I can see, up to 1955, when this brief was filed before the Gordon commission by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories there had been no other alternative really considered seriously in so far as this rail route was concerned.
I should say this. In the last 35 years thousands of people have settled in the area from Grimshaw north on the express understanding that this railroad would be built, and that when built it would go through the territory of the Peace river country north

from Grimshaw and into the Northwest Territories and Great Slave lake, following that particular route.
During the course of the hearings of this commission it was my privilege to act as counsel for the boards of trade and the chambers of commerce of the Peace river country and to ask people who lived in that area to come forward, or their children, to give some indication as to the reasons which had prompted their settlement in this area. As a result I received hundreds of letters-in fact, I could safely say they ran into thousands-[DOT] from people who had settled, or whose fathers and mothers had settled in this area, on the specific and distinct understanding that when this railway would be built this would be the route which would be chosen. Consequently, it came as a very distinct shock when toward the latter part of 1957 or early in 1958 it became apparent to many people in our country that serious consideration had been given to another area and to another route. From what I have discovered I am satisfied that this change in planning came into existence or was considered sometime between the latter part of 1955 and the early part of 1957. I think I have ample evidence for stating this, and it is demonstrated in part by these points.
During the hearings of the Manning royal commission as to the route of the railway to Great Slave lake evidence was given by a man called Denney, of the Denney Logging Company, who stated that in 1956 when he was considering applying for timber limits in Wood Buffalo park, which is the park to which my hon. friend from Athabasca made reference, he had been told by one government official that this railroad was definitely planned to go through Wood Buffalo park, which was the eastern route. His evidence also was to the effect that there were also other government officials, probably more highly placed, who had given him some information, but when pressed on examination he refused to give those names.
I might say here, Mr. Chairman, that the man who gave this information to Denney, a man who is called, I think, Evans Essex or Essex Evans-at this time my memory fails me as to his name but he was a government official; I am told his last name was Essex- held a position of some substance in the park. In the fall of 1956 he left his position with the department of northern affairs and became manager of this United States lumber company, the Denney Logging Company. At the same hearing a pamphlet was presented consisting of maps and sketches which dealt with the future development of Forth Smith, which lies in the vicinity of the eastern route. This publication clearly established on one

particular sketch that a railway line was projected to go through Fort Smith, and showed evidence of yards and a station which were planned for Fort Smith. This document came out some time in June or July of 1957 and could only have been prepared on information gathered together and obtained over a period of many months preceding it. It clearly indicates just what government thinking had been in the months prior to the summer of 1957.
Finally-this is the third point that I shall present to the committee-although I have others-in 1957, the railway companies, obviously acting in connection with government understanding and no doubt on a decision to which the government of that day was privy, dispatched an engineer for the purpose of considering various routes, but instead of directing his attention to the route which had been the western route first planned and understood to be the one which would be chosen, this engineer directed a lot of his attention to a survey of the eastern route. For this reason, so far as I am concerned, I am satisfied beyond any reasonable doubt that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, at that time under the administration of Mr. Lesage who has now gone on to greater rewards in the province of Quebec, decided to abandon the people of the Peace river country, forget the promises that had been made to them and, under some kind of collusive understanding with the railway companies, build this railroad along the eastern route. The result of this, of course, would have been to leave the railways to charge whatever they thought the traffic would bear.

speechtext:
This is all strong circumstantial evidence. All of the facts of which I have spoken can be found by an examination of the transcript of the proceedings of the Manning royal commission, as to the route to Great Slave lake, which are to be found in the library. The three specific facts to which I have referred are mentioned. If the hon. member wishes, I might be able to assist him in finding them.
As I was starting to say, Mr. Chairman, my belief is that this would have been a fine thing for the railway companies and if I were a railroad man I might have said that this was the route to choose. There would be no competition and they could charge what in their opinion the traffic would bear. Again, it
Supply-Northern Affairs would have benefited one or two companies and a few individuals who stood to gain by the choice of this eastern route, but it would have left betrayed the many thousands of people who, as a result of the promises made over a period of years, had reason to expect that when this railroad was built it would be built through the Peace river country.
I mentioned something about logging operations in Wood Buffalo park to which the hon. member for Athabasca also referred. I want to make it crystal clear, Mr. Chairman, that I have no constitutional objection to what can be established as a reasonable amount of logging being done in that park according to proper logging practices. However, I do believe I am entitled to take exception to all the shenanigans that occurred with regard to this particular project.
In the first instance, the berths in respect of which this logging was undertaken were berths which were given by way of order in council following certain amendments to the National Parks Act. Two years ago, I believe it was, I had occasion to comment on that procedure in the house. I said that in my professional opinion there was very great doubt as to whether these orders in council were valid. It may well be that the departmental solicitors have given opinions to the contrary. I have been able in the past to substantiate my professional opinion, at times, against that of the departmental solicitors. Until I have been shown to the contrary it is still my feeling that there is a great cloud of uncertainty and doubt about the validity of these orders in council.
In the second place, these particular orders in council had the effect, when implemented and when certain assignments had been given, of granting to two corporations, one of which was a United States corporation which had recently come into Canada, the entire rights with respect to more than 1.5 billion board-feet of merchantable timber in this park. I believe that this amount constitutes almost the total amount of merchantable timber in the park. Now, this United States firm came in with machinery which, I am told, was not suitable for the purpose for which it was brought here. The company had difficulty in meeting its obligations and probably had some difficulty in meeting its commitments to the government.
For the life of me I cannot see why, if we are going to do any logging in our national parks, we should have to import a United States firm to do it. I feel that all this was done to lend strength and colour to the reasons assigned in justification of this eastern route. It was done in the spirit of the-public-be-damned and constituted a grave

Supply-Northern Affairs infraction not only of the spirit but the letter of the law in connection with the operation of our national parks.
Before I leave this subject may I state that the preambles to these orders in council giving reasons for the allowance of this exploitation set out that the timber in these areas was largely mature and over-mature timber. This issue came up before the Manning commission and there was filed with the commission a thesis by a man named Thorp, a gentleman who had been employed for some years in the national parks, which he had written in connection with his admission to the professional foresters' association in British Columbia. I do not have sufficient knowledge to interpret this brief but it was interpreted to the distinguished members of this commission as constituting a complete negation of that theory. In fact, the professional forester who gave evidence interpreting this thesis to the commission said that there was no larger percentage of mature and overmature timber in this park than there was in any of the other areas east of the Rocky mountains.
Probably this is all water under the bridge now, Mr. Chairman, and I am compelled to bring it up only by reason of the suggestions which have been advanced by the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member who spoke yesterday. These hon. members were critical of the achievements for which this government has been responsible in connection with northern development. I might add that the people in my part of the country will always regard with esteem the action of the Prime Minister and this government in permitting this commission to hold hearings so that we would have an opportunity to ventilate the facts. It has always been my belief that given a just and proper case with strong evidence, and a determination to pursue it, justice usually results.
The commission has now decided, two to one, in favour of the western route. This is a good decision and I am not going into the detailed reasons for it. The report is there for all hon. members to see. The decision of the government to implement it is a wise and proper decision. Immediately after the estimates were passed in December of this year appropriating money for the surveys to be made, the machinery was set in action. Since then a great deal of work has been done. I am informed by what we in the north call moccasin telegraph that the results which have so far been achieved have been quite remarkable and more than justify the decision. Along this route adequate supplies of gravel have been found to be used as ballast. There is more than sufficient lumber from

which ties can be fashioned. It has been discovered, as we have always maintained, that there are large amounts of merchantable timber along the western route far in excess of the amount that might be found along the eastern route, even including what could be found in Wood Buffalo national park. The attention which has been directed to the Peace river area and the north generally as a result of the decision of this government has been quite remarkable.
Just the other day I received a copy of a local newspaper which indicated very substantial reserves of iron ore in the Hines Creek-Clear Hills area of the Peace river country had been found and which would more than likely be developed in the not too distant future. This was, I suggest, an indirect result of the decision of the government to proceed with this railroad. There are areas of agricultural land along this eastern route which I think constitute the last great reservoir of such lands in North America. I am satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that *when this decision is finally implemented and this railroad is completed the present population of the Peace river country, which includes part of the area inhabited by those people who live in the constituency of the hon. member for Cariboo and in the area which goes into the lower part of Mackenzie, will be augmented to not less than half a million people by 1975. This is not idle conjecture. I could pinpoint the places where communities will be established, where towns will grow, where lumber operations will flourish, where there is natural gas and petroleum. These are not pipe dreams; these are not visions. These are actual facts which have been brought to the knowledge of the people during the course of the last few years.
I wish to make one more point in connection with the building of this railway. I grant that it will help, and it is intended mainly to help, the people in the Northwest Territories. It will have an immeasurably beneficial effect on the people in my constituency. Primarily, however, the bread and butter motive for constructing the railroad is to enable the ore produced at Pine Point mine to be brought down to Trail to the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company for processing. I think we are at the stage where time is of the essence. I understand, and I am supported in this by statements which have been appearing in the press, that Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company at Trail depends to some extent for its economic production on the presence of what are known as smelter residues. These smelter residues will shortly be exhausted. It is for that reason that Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, which holds a large interest in the Pine

Point mine, is most anxious that the railroad be completed and the minerals brought down from Pine Point to Trail. The failure to do that may well result in the company having to obtain custom ore, possibly from outside of Canada. I think that would be a great tragedy and I therefore urge the government, particularly the minister, to push ahead with this project as quickly as possible.
I recognize that we are in a difficult period in so far as railroads are concerned. However, it has been my submission, and I urged this two years ago, that this railroad should be constructed as a special railroad within the meaning of the Railway Act. It should not be compelled under the normal provisions of the Railway Act to carry passengers and to submit to the other more costly procedures which in the past went with railroad construction and operation. This is simply and purely a development railroad. It should be built with that fact in mind and it should be built as soon as possible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This is the first opportunity I have had to congratulate the minister on his new appointment. He is a well liked and well respected member of this House of Commons and a man of high principles. I wish him well in his new responsibilities.
I rise in my place today to say a few words about only one subject that comes under the minister's responsibility. I refer to tourism which is an important industry, of course, to Canada and of particular importance in our area. I realize that it can be said that 1961 looks to be a promising year and for this, of course, we are glad. We can refer to modest increases over the years. I have just spent some time with some of the important leaders in the tourist industry of this country who were recently brought together in North Bay, and I can assure you that all is not well in the industry. I should like to refer to one aspect only today. This is a trend which is growing successively worse with each passing year.
This aspect of tourism, this growing of the deficit in our travel account is a matter of genuine concern, I know, to the government and to all thoughtful Canadians. I should like to refer to the Bank of Canada report of 1960. At page 44 it deals with non-merchandise transactions in the balance of international payments on current account. In this respect I should like to point out that Canadians spent $215 million more in 1960 abroad than tourists spent in Canada. This is a situation that has worsened to this $215 million deficit position from a position in 1950 of a surplus on travel account of $49 million. As a matter of interest, we could go back to 1939 when there was a surplus in this account of $68 million.
90205-6-247
Supply-Northern Affairs
I am not going to lecture the minister this afternoon on the importance of tourism or remind him that today travel is the fastest expanding industry in the world or tell him that it is the second best source of United States dollars for Canada. However, I am convinced that he must persuade his colleagues that greater effort and spending will have to be made in view of this trend to which I have referred, namely this deficit in our travel account.
Canada has one of the world's lowest per tourist expenditures on tourist promotion in other countries. When we look at the facts we find that Bermuda spends $12.50 per tourist. In the countries of Europe the average spending is $9.50 per tourist. When we realize these facts, and when they are viewed in the light of this new development and in the light of world competition, they make our efforts seem quite inadequate, when we consider that this year there will be perhaps 30 million visits to this country and that the total amount of money covered in vote 303 is $2,687,000, which means less than 10 cents per visit. I am not holding this up as a comparison with the figures I have just used. I make the statement only to point out what I consider to be the inadequate approach to this whole problem that has developed in the tourist industry in this country and throughout the world.
It is a matter of genuine concern that travel expenditure by United States citizens abroad -and this matter was referred to earlier today I believe-was up 300 per cent in the last ten years and yet travel expenditures by United States citizens in Canada is only up approximately 20 odd per cent in the same period.
We must also look at the other side of the coin. Expenditures by Canadians outside of Canada are now four times greater than they were in 1948 and they are still rising. To reduce this trend is not an easy task. I think we all recognize that fact having in mind our geography, climate and economic conditions. Quite apart from the understandable pull of winter sunshine resorts it must be realized that world wide competition for the tourist dollar is growing every year. Our United States friends have been alert to this competition and as early as 1958 a special report to the president-I think it was referred to as the Randall report-formed the basis of extensive "See America First" and "Come to America" national tourist programs. We in Canada are losing ground. The annual deficit in our travel account as I have mentioned, has now reached $215 million. Only a vigorous and extensive program directed at tourists at home and abroad can turn the tide. To ensure the success of such a program we

Supply-Northern Affairs must pursue an intensified course of raising our standards with respect to facilities and services if we are to expect our visitors from abroad to return or indeed our own people to accept enthusiastically a "See Canada First" or "Know Canada Better" program.
Tourism has grown tremendously in the past few years. Increased earnings, a shorter work week, longer holidays with pay, have all contributed greatly to making travel available to most people rather than to just the wealthy few as was the case in pre-war days. Tourism helps all segments of the economy. When people travel they spend their money on food and lodging, transportation, entertainment and a host of other services. Whether one operates a hotel or motel, a resort, a restaurant, a grocery store or is a manufacturer of sports clothes or equipment or operates a department store or sells gas or oil or even collects taxes, all benefit from the tourist dollar. Yes, tourism is everybody's business and it affects every area in this country. I believe there is a growing realization of this fact.
Considerable effort is being poured into the industry at the local, regional and provincial levels. In my own immediate area of Nipissing, which is a real vacationers' paradise, tourist spending amounts to $6 million annually. Many of our tourist operators are doing an excellent promotion job within their financial capabilities. Just the other evening at this meeting in North Bay to which I referred earlier many organizations such as N.O.T.A., N.O.O.A., Northern Ontario Outfitters Association; A.T.R.O., Associated Tourist Resorts of Ontario; O.T.C.A., Ontario Tourist Court Association and the important B.O.T.A., Board of Ontario Travel Associations were represented. These people are making a great contribution. In fact, these names are starting to sound like the various agencies of the United Nations. Of course, I should not forget our own North Bay Lakeshore Resorts Association.
I believe, however, that more federal leadership should be provided and is needed if Canada is to reverse the deficit trend in our tourist industry. Once we agree that tourism is everyone's business there should be a growing pooling of ideas and a greater spending and planning for the promotion of that industry.
We could persuade our visitors to stay longer. We could urge more visitors to come to Canada. We could urge more people to come to Canada in the winter time, and we could try harder to induce Canadians to spend their holidays in Canada.
A tourist does not have to be a person from another country. If 15 per cent of the Canadians who are now spending their holidays in other lands could be induced to spend

their holidays in Canada it would wipe out the yearly travel deficit which we have with the rest of the world.
Advertising alone will not solve this problem. Very often the emphasis is just on the spending of money. Surely this is not the answer. I believe there is room for more prudent spending, more pooling of ideas and a great opportunity for leadership at the federal level in this important industry.
Before resuming my seat I wish to refer to two further items. It will be recalled that last year representatives were sent to Europe to investigate the tourist potential from that part of the world because of the resurgence of the European economy. It was a very wise move to tap as much as possible this important market in this field. I hope the minister will say something about the actions of the federal government in this regard.
I should also like to refer to one other matter which I raised in the house earlier this session. I refer to the concern that some of us felt when President Kennedy asked congress to reduce to $100 from $500 the value of tax free goods United States' tourists could take back to their country at any one time. I think we were justified in feeling some concern at that time. There was an article in the Ottawa Journal of February 7 this year which refers to the attitude of the minister. The article was written by Gordon Dewar and says:
Little effect should be felt in the Canadian tourist industry if the U.S. congress should approve spending cuts for American tourists asked by President Kennedy Monday.
The article continues:
This, at least, is the opinion of federal government officials, including northern affairs minister Dinsdale, whose department is responsible for tourism in Canada.
An article was written by Harold Morrison of the Canadian Press. The article originated in Washington and appeared in the February 20 issue of the Ottawa Citizen. It refers to the attitude of the Prime Minister and says:
He-
That is the Prime Minister:
-had heard no objections in Canada to Kennedy's proposal to reduce the American tax free exemption on tourist goods to $100 from $500.
There was another story, again originating in Washington, which appeared in the March 7 issue of the Ottawa Citizen:
A congressional committee has deferred action on President Kennedy's proposal to reduce the maximum duty free allowance on tourist goods to $100 from $500 to permit further clarification of the Canadian position ...
It will be recalled that the Minister of Finance, in answer to a question I asked,

indicated that representations had finally been made by the minister when he visited Washington later in March.
I think we are justified in being concerned about this apparent lack of policy and the various positions and attitudes taken by this government in this very important matter. I hope the minister will have something to say on this subject.
Surely this will have a serious psychological effect on our relations with the United States in this regard. We are spending $100 million in excess of United States spending in Canada. Surely there is no justification for this action by the United States as far as Canada is concerned. I hope the minister will say a few words on this important matter in the course of his remarks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is very active in my riding I know it will come as no surprise to the minister if I rise on his estimates to discuss his department's relations with my constituency and also to suggest to him ways in which his department can be of service in the future to Inverness-Richmond as it has been in the past.
However, I should first of all like to express my congratulations to the minister who has taken over this department so recently and has already shown such a firm and intelligent hand in its administration and in advancing the very good work begun by his predecessor, and indeed opening up new approaches himself.
I understand that the minister plans to come to Nova Scotia this summer. I must say that the people of my province will be very glad to welcome him and certainly I look forward very much to the opportunity to show him around Cape Breton Highlands national park in North Inverness. I know my colleague from Cape Breton North and Victoria will also look forward to that opportunity.
Also I should like to show the minister Fort Louisbourg in another part of my riding, which I know he would like to examine very fully when he has time to do so.
I should like to show him the famous Cabot trail, which is perhaps one of the most famous scenic spots in the eastern provinces, and I want to show him why so many tourists over the years have been attracted to this very wonderful part of Nova Scotia. He will drive over the new road that is almost completed and over the trail that will be completed by this July. I recall some 25 years ago when I first went over the Cabot trail the road was so narrow that there was scarcely room for one car. If you met somebody on the 90205-6-2474
Supply-Northern Affairs road you had to back down to a spot that was wide enough to allow the other car to go by. This was along the banks of a precipice in many cases and appeared very dangerous, even to me in those days.
I should also like to have the minister note what the Cape Breton Highlands national park has meant to the development of the tourist industry not only in Inverness country but indeed the whole of Nova Scotia. Our tourist industry has grown by leaps and bounds in the last few years and no small part of the reason for this is to be found in the attraction of the Cape Breton Highlands national park. The new camp sites built by the department and the general increase in facilities over the last two or three years have provided extra services for visitors to the park, and these services are very welcome. Indeed, the build-up of the tourist industry in that area stands as proof of the wisdom of the investment that has been made to date in the park.
Last year the registrations at the Cape Breton Highlands national park were 227,262. Every year recently there has been a big increase in the number of registrations. When we realize how important the tourist industry is, particularly to Cape Breton, we can understand what it has meant to this part of the country to have this very important and wise investment in the area. Every Nova Scotian town has a most important investment in the tourist industry, in terms of motels, hotels, restaurants and similar facilities. Nova Scotia is building up a very worth-while tourist industry and I am optimistic that it will continue to grow. We are very close to the vast population of the eastern seaboard of the United States and many of these people like to come to Nova Scotia, and they are coming in increasing numbers, to escape the heat of their cities and to feel the cool seabreezes of the maritime summer. I should like to compliment the minister and his department on the great increase in advertising respecting Nova Scotia. I am sure the increased money spent has had a lot to do with the increase we are seeing today in the number of tourists from the United States.
I may say also that in an area where the principal occupations have been fishing and lumbering the employment that has been provided to the local people in building up the park has been very welcome. The area around Cheticamp and North Inverness generally has presented in recent years a much more prosperous appearance as a result of the extra money available in those communities through the payrolls of the department. I hope this will continue, and, again, I assure the minister that every dollar spent in developing parks such as the Cape Breton

Supply-Northern Affairs national park is a good investment for Canada and the means of providing a worthwhile attraction for the tourists who will come to visit us.
As the tourist industry grows it will be necessary to continue the campsite building program and to assist in other ways to provide recreation and accommodation facilities in the park. I think it would be beneficial if a swimming pool were built on the Cheticamp side of the park. There is at present a golf course at Ingonish on the other side of the park but the time is coming when we shall need a second, and I suggest that this should be near Cheticamp.
When he is visiting I should like the minister to take a look at Cheticamp island because I believe that the acquisition of this land, or part of it, would be a valuable addition to present resources. This should be done without delay, because in a few years time the land might not be as readily available as it is today. We are going to need more campsites and recreation facilities, and Cheticamp island with its fine beaches and its tie-in with the rest of the park would be a natural addition.
Before leaving this topic I should like to pay a tribute to the superintendent of the park, Mr. F. C. Browning. He is a man well liked by all the citizens of the area and by the men who work for him. I know he has at heart the building up of the park and that he devotes a lot of time to planning and seeking out ways in which the park can be made a greater tourist attraction and of more use to the people of the surrounding area.
I should like, now, to address to the minister a few remarks on the subject of Louis-bourg. I am proud to have this famous historic spot in my riding and I know the minister will appreciate that this is the fourth occasion on which I have brought up this matter in the house. I should like to express my thanks to boards of trade in the area and to other associations which have from time to time sent me resolutions, and sent resolutions to the minister, regarding Louisburg, or who have sent briefs suggesting ways in which this great Canadian monument could be refurbished. In 1963 Louisburg will be commemorating its two hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the founding of the town which, as all hon. members know, was first laid down in 1713. In 1958, at the bicentennial ceremonies, a large group of people turned out at Louisburg to take part, and I am sure that by 1963 as many as 100,000 people will be on hand. I think it is important that these people, who will have come from far and near to the fortress town, may have a chance to see there something which will give them a proper reward for their visit,

and that they may have a chance to carry away with them something of the story of this historic place.
There can be no doubt as to the historic importance of Louisburg. William Pitt referred to it as the "key to European power in the new world" during the days of the conflict between France and England out of which this country was born. Every day I meet Canadians from all parts of the nation who ask me: what is being done about Louisburg? Interest is widespread. Moreover, interest is not confined to Canada; it extends to those who live in the New England states, since many men from New England took part in the siege of 1745. Louisburg not only played a part in British history but in United States history as well. Further, I feel that apart altogether from the economic value which may attach to Louisburg, we Canadians are too prone to neglect the history of our nation; we spend too little time seeing to it that people learn the story of our national life. Some of the tales of Louisburg are of the greatest in Canadian history; the course of events which was shaped then has altered the lives of all Canadians today and, certainly, the bald phrases of the history books alone can never succeed in showing just what part this old fortress played in the early life of Canada.
I should like to emphasize the need for further expenditure at Louisburg while expressing my thanks for what has already been done there. I understand that this year there will be a number of guides there who will be familiar with the history of the spot and who will be able to tell visitors something about the Louisburg story. And a fulltime curator is to be appointed to take over the museum. Economically speaking I am certain our tourist industry will be greatly enhanced by the development of Louisburg. At present, only about one tenth of the people who go to the Cape Breton Highlands national park make a visit to Louisburg. Building up the site will bring many people down from Cabot trail to the southern side of the island and, encourage them to spend another two or three days on the island of Cape Breton.
Along with this I think that a new road should be constructed from Louisburg to St. Peters along the southern shore of Cape Breton and Richmond counties to open up an area which is known to very few and which is not now served by a good road. This would provide a circular route for tourists coming in at Port Hawkesbury and over the Cabot trail, and would allow them to leave from St. Peters. It would provide tourist

interest in that part of the province which certainly does not now have its share of visitors.
I know that the construction of highways is not within the province of the minister, but I hope some arrangement can be worked out with the province of Nova Scotia in the interest of bringing more people to fortress Louisburg and of the general development of the area.
I am not going to list the structures which I think should be built at Louisburg, or make suggestions in regard to restoration, as I know the minister is in possession of two or three briefs from the associated boards of trade of Cape Breton island in regard to this subject, as well as briefs from organizations in the town of Louisburg itself. I do think, however, that in time substantial restoration of a portion of the French town should take place.
It is important at once to acquire more land for the historic site. I am sad to say that Wolfe's Landing at Louisburg, which is east of the fortress, is not now within the historic site grounds. But the acquiring of a few extra acres would make it possible to bring this particularly interesting spot within the enclosure. I am sure that the department will wish to do this so as to preserve this site properly for all Canadians.
At this particular time, when new employment will be badly needed in Cape Breton Island, I would suggest to the minister that all possible steps should be taken to put under way, as soon as possible, a large construction program at Louisburg. Not only would the investment be a very sound one, as I have said, but the work done at the site, because of its nature, must be done by hand. It is the type of work that employs a large number of people and would provide assistance to many who will be out of work this summer if the proposed closing of some Dosco mines cannot be avoided. I urge the minister to begin to develop the Louisburg site as soon as possible for economic reasons as well as to properly display this very important historic monument in Canada.
