speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the item carries I would like to ask for the indulgence of the committee for a few moments. We have heard hon. members this afternoon advocating various ways and means of increasing the flow of tourists to this country. We have heard suggestions in regard to the establishment and restoration of various historic sites and monuments in different parts of the country. It is in this regard that I would like to direct the minister's attention because, in my mind, there is no better way
Supply-Northern Affairs of graphically telling the story of a people than by means of historic sites, relics and monuments.
I would suggest that Canada abounds with history from coast to coast. All too often historic areas in perhaps more remote parts of the country tend to be forgotten in favour of the more well-known and accessible areas in the central part of Canada. In 1955 the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, on behalf of the government of Canada, proceeded with the establishment of a historic site on the easternmost tip of Canada which is, as a matter of fact, the easternmost tip of North America. This site, which is now under development as a national historic park, is equal in historic significance and import to the plains of Abraham in Quebec and other historic sites in the southern part of Ontario. This is the site of the last armed conflict in North America between the French and English during the seven years' war. It was at this site in the 1770's that the French and English fought for possession of North America. It was in the year 1705 that construction of a fort by the then British garrison was undertaken at this historic site. It was completed in the year 1711. It has been called the "Queen's fort", taking its name from Queen Anne, the then reigning monarch of Great Britain.
After this site was taken over as a national historic park in 1955 there followed a very slow period of development. I am sorry to say that to this day, some five or six years later, this historic site of national significance is sadly underdeveloped.
Regrettably, a few months ago one of the oldest landmarks in Canada, built in 1705, was destroyed by fire. With all due respect to my hon. friend, in whose constituency fort Louisbourg is located, I would suggest that this fort preceded Louisbourg fort by several years. As I say, in 1705 this grand old building was erected and in 1960 was burned down. As a result of the Department of Northern Affairs and Natural Resources in its wisdom evicting the old gentleman and his family who had lived in this building for many years, it was left without a custodian and, through lack of proper supervision, or perhaps as a result of carelessness, this historic site of national significance has been destroyed.
I would ask the minister to tell the committee when he expects Signal Hill historic park will be completed. Since 1955, when it was commenced, only a relatively minor paving program and some restoration to Cabot tower has taken place. I would suggest for the benefit of hon. members that this historic site is of interest from the point of view of contemporary history, because of the

Supply-Northern Affairs fact that in 1901 the first Marconi wireless message from Cornwall, England, was received at this site. I say this to illustrate the fact that here is a site of tremendous significance in the history of Canada, both in its early history and in its later development. I would suggest to those responsible in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources that they immediately initiate a stepped up program for the completion of this area and for the restoration of that part of the Queen's fort which was destroyed by vandals, I believe, a few months ago for want of a proper custodian and a watchman.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I submit there are historical sites in Canada of less significance which are fully developed. I do not want to be specific but, for example, I hold in my hand a booklet put out by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources through the Canadian travel bureau on Fort Malden national historic park at Amherstburg, Ontario. I have had the privilege of visiting this site. Some of my hon. friends from eastern Canada should visit some of the sites in Ontario and see how they are really and properly developed, what a tourist attraction they are and what a sense of pride they are to those residents of this part of Canada. On the cover of this booklet which commemorates this site of a historical nature, but in my submission of not the same historical importance as Signal Hill park, there is a very apt quotation, and I shall close with it in the hope that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who has brought so much zeal, vigour and enthusiasm to his new post, will give the attention that they justly deserve and demand to the historical sites of Canada. The quotation is by Joseph Howe, and it reads as follows:
A wise nation preserves its record, gathers up its muniments, decorates the tombs of its illustrious dead, repairs its great public structures and fosters national pride and love of country by perpetual reference to the sacrifices and glories of the past.

When the Seven Nations Indians heard about this a request was made to me and to the local council to approach the federal government with a view to recognizing the significance of those bones and to establish an ossuary and a plaque. Several ambitious schemes have been advanced along the lines of providing perhaps a replica of an early Indian village similar to the type of thing found in the national museum. I understand that many persons are still interested in that aspect of the development, but I would appreciate it if the minister could bring us up to date on the progress of the Scarborough ossuary.

I rise on a point of order, if I may. There has been a long standing custom in this house over a great many years, certainly all the time that I have been here, before the advent of this government, that when a public bill standing in the name of a private member was asked to stand it was automatically stood at the request of the member in whose name the bill appeared. This was done time after time and no question was raised as to this procedure. I think the practice was a correct one and that public bills in the name of private members are in fact private member's bills. In my opinion the procedure of the house from five o'clock to six o'clock should not be based on rules set out by the government or requests made by the government. Since this government took office, and in the last couple of years particularly, there has been a disposition to stand bills such as these first by request of the member in whose name the bill appears or by the request of the whip for the party concerned. Then, the Speaker would say, "at the request of the government," and the bill would stand in a routine fashion.
However, a week ago when Bill No. C-19, standing in my name, was called, I asked that it stand. I will agree that just a few minutes before I had not been too co-operative during the consideration of item No. 1 of the post office estimates. We are not always cooperative. I think sometimes hon. members on both sides dig in their heels. It was the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pick-ersgill) who initiated the procedure by pointing out rule 19. At that time the house leader, I take it because of what had happened a few moments before, said the government was not requesting that this bill stand. I immediately proceeded with it.
I had hoped today, however, that as a courtesy to me, this bill might have been allowed to stand without prejudice to its position on the order paper. I was informed this procedure would not be followed and that unless I was prepared to proceed with it at this time the government would not request that it stand and the bill would have to go to the bottom of the order paper. With the large number of public bills on the order paper this would mean that, for all practical purposes, the bill would be dead for this session.
Small Loans Act
My point of order is this: The rules have not been changed on this question. A practice of the house had been built up over many years, I think an excellent practice, whereby public bills standing in the name of private members would stand on the request of the private member with an indication that the government was agreeable. I suggest that the government is making a mistake in the rule that is now going to be laid down, as I understand, that private members' bills will not be allowed to stand. I feel this rule will not aid orderly discussion. I think it will make it difficult for us if we wish to stand two or three bills in order to debate a bill, say, on capital punishment in which all the members of the house may be interested. I understand that the house leader is laying down this as the practice the government will follow in the future, that private bills will not be stood at the request of the government.
I feel this rule amounts to contempt of the private members' hour. I think it shows the government is becoming very arrogant and very dictatorial in its attitude. It is now, by this means, wielding the big stick. For the first time in all the years I have been in the house the government, by this arbitrary rule, is going to say that from now on if a bill stands at the top of the order paper and is not moved, then it gets the guillotine. I suggest that on the basis of co-operation in the house, the need for some give and take, this is a stupid attitude the government is taking and a course that should not be followed.

The hon. gentleman, as usual, has used very extravagant language to describe the adherence to the rules which have been in existence for years. This issue was first raised on March 13, 1959, by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin). The hon. member for Nickel Belt, as I understand it, is not a supporter of this government. He rose to a point of order at that time to the effect that standing order 19 required either that the motion for second reading of a bill must be proceeded with or that the bill should lose its precedence on the order paper. Mr. Speaker, in a lengthy statement at that time, indicated the way in which the rule had been applied and then said that the proper application of the rule required that bills should stand only at the request of the government. Subsequent to that, when a bill stood it stood at the request of the government with the house leader so indicating.
The last occasion on which this question was raised was, as the hon. gentleman said, last Friday. Was it a supporter of the government who raised the issue? It was not.

He said: I am pleased to move once again a bill which has for its purpose the lowering of interest rates which may be charged by small loans companies in this country. I have had the opportunity to move similar bills back over the years. The first time I moved a bill in these terms was in 1954. At that time it received some support in the house. The Conservative opposition in the house of that day was silent and non-com-mital. The Liberal government followed the practice of putting on a cabinet minister who set forward the position taken by the government and, although this was not always the case at that time, they did follow the practice of talking the bill out.
I do not think I have been associated with any public bill or with any cause at all in a public bill which has received wider support in this nation than the contention that small loan companies are fleecing the public, that their interest rates are exorbitant and that it is time, in the interests of the consumer and the borrower, that parliament should act to further control the rates of interest which can be charged by small loan companies. When this bill was moved on a former occasion it created a great deal of stir in the country and aroused a great deal of public support.

In 1956, I think it was, the minister of finance introduced a bill which was eventually incorporated into the Small Loans Act which extended to a large extent the area of control of interest rates that may be charged by small loans companies. Before that time the control amounted to a ceiling of 2 per cent per month on loans up to $500. With the passage of this particular amendment at that time, on loans up to $300 the 2 per cent provision was allowed or permitted; on loans in excess of $300 but less than $1,000, 1 per cent was provided and for unpaid balances in excess of $1,000 half of 1 per cent per month was the ceiling provided. There is no doubt in my mind that this step forward saved the consumers of this country many millions of dollars.
We in this group are asking by this measure that the area of control should now be further extended and that action should be taken by parliament to save the consumers and borrowers of this country millions of dollars in exorbitant interest rates. I have been discouraged, or, perhaps I should say, I have been disappointed by the attitude taken by the Conservative members in general. In the past they have not been sympathetic to these proposals. They have argued that in a free enterprise economy you should let the buyer beware; that it is the fault of the borrower if these things happen and that parliament should not be asked to increase its jurisdiction in order to protect the ordinary Canadian borrower or consumer. Recently, however, there have been signs of an encouraging change in the attitude of at least some of the hon. members who sit opposite.
A week ago when I proposed Bill No. C-19 which would make it necessary by law for small loans companies to set forth in their advertising the interest rates that could be charged I received a good deal of vocal support from certain members of the Conservative party though this support did not extend to the point of allowing a vote to be taken. Although I said to the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MaeLellan) that he had killed the bill by extended faint praise- by talking it out-the tenor of his remarks was more favourable than were the comments of some of the other members of the Conservative party on former occasions. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond had this to say at one point in his remarks:
I support the general principle of this bill. I should like to see the matter examined further by a committee of this house.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) who has probably been the most active and most talkative member on the government side with regard to bills of this

nature has been something of a killer member on the government side of the house. His job seems to have been to do anything he could to kill these bills, and he has been very successful. He has helped himself. He has set an example to members around him. He has talked on these bills. He has pointed out weaknesses, some real, no doubt, but most of them imaginary. He has spent a large part of his time making certain that these bills were talked out and killed. However, I noticed in that hon. member also what I took to be a change of emphasis in his statement of a week ago. He seemed at that time to have something more in mind than simply running down the provisions of the bill. He seemed to take a more constructive attitude and I hope this indicates a change in the attitude not only of the hon. member but on the part of the majority of the members on that side of the house. I would hope that this means the government will, in future, take a more lenient view to the proposals put forward in this and other bills I have moved regarding interest rates in Canada.
The hon. member for Davenport had the following to say, as reported at page 3698 of Hansard of April 14, 1961:
Judging by the various bills that have been introduced in the house and the information put before the house within the last few years by members on all sides. I would say the time has come when the whole matter of interest, the Interest Act and the Small Loans Act, as well as this proposed legislation should be reviewed in toto.
He went on to say that there should be a periodic review, and this review should be undertaken by the banking and commerce committee. I hope that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bell) will follow me in this debate, and I would express the hope that when he makes his comments he will confirm the statement that was made by the hon. member for Davenport. I hope he will make it clear to the house that the government is prepared to take a more lenient attitude toward this measure. I would also make a plea that the government refer this bill, and the other bills I have on the order paper dealing with interest rates, the ceiling on interest rates, and advertising, to the banking and commerce committee this session so that we may have a thorough review of the interest provisions in these acts, and so they may be changed to provide greater protection to the consumers in this country.
There exists a provision in the Small Loans Act providing for control, as set forth in the legislation, on loans up to a maximum of $1,500. In respect of loans over $1,500 there is no control, so that a small loans company making a loan of $1,501 is able to charge

of $10 million. That company has subscribed and paid up cash amounting to $1 million. According to the 1958 statistics that company made a net profit for the year of $5,230,000 on its paid up capital of $1 million, with income earned on small loans to the tune of $12.2 million.

This fact may no longer influence hon. members opposite, but the two large firms-Household Finance and Beneficial Finance-have made approximately 70 per cent of the loans in this country, and are controlled outside of this country.
I suggest that, in every respect, this bill and the other bills I have moved in this regard, warrant the support of all members of the house. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would first like to set the record straight. We heard the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) at the beginning of his speech, shortly after another issue was settled at five o'clock, make the suggestions that this bill had been presented to the house during the past five, six or seven years, and that it had been talked out. The hon. member has made his speech and perhaps he will be good enough to allow me to make mine.
The first bill was presented on April 17, 1959. Having read the debate for that year in that regard I can see why the hon. member for Assiniboia was somewhat irritated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Smith). The hon. member for Winnipeg North made some rather unflattering remarks about the amount of research that had not been done by the hon. member for Assiniboia in presenting the measure at that time. Since my time is short I will not repeat them, but I certainly endorse the remarks found in that particular debate.
The fact is, we have an emotional issue before us this afternoon. A debate on an emotional issue always presents an opportunity for members to rise and fulminate against

the money lending section of the population. If we intended to be truly political we could certainly back up those remarks without bothering to find out the consequences of any bill we passed. I think if this measure were passed the moneylenders in this country would be automatically out of business. I might say that I am in favour of that particular course because I have, fortunately, not had occasion to go to the small loans companies so far, and hope I never will. However, perhaps more than a million individuals have had occasion to do business with them.
The purpose of this bill is really to reduce from 2 per cent per month to 1 per cent per month the interest paid on small loans. At present the rate is 2 per cent per month up to $300; then 1 per cent from $300 to $1,000; and then one half of one per cent from $1,000 to $1,500, and there the operations of the act cease. Therefore, the effect would be to reduce the amount from 2 per cent per month to 1 per cent per month on all loans up to the figure of $300.
The difficulty I find in this bill-and I should like to support it-is to know just what effect it will have. I tried to make some rough calculations. I calculated that perhaps this would reduce the amount of interest paid to small loans operators by as much as $15 million or perhaps $20 million a year. Then, looking at Mr. MacGregor's report on small loans companies, moneylenders, for the year ended December 31, 1959, I found that the gross profit of small loans companies was something of the order of $15.9 million for the year 1959. For the previous year, 1958, it had been around $15.1 million. If my calculations are correct, and unfortunately I cannot claim very much accuracy for them, it would mean that the amount of gross profit, or the profit to run the business, would practically disappear and perforce the companies themselves would also have to disappear. I am not saying this is a particularly bad thing, at least in my case, but it might be bad for Canadians who were forced to forsake this particular group to borrow their money and go to some other particular group.
You see, Mr. Speaker, the difficulty is that we have no figures in Mr. MacGregor's excellent report-and it is an excellent report and well worth reading-showing the amount of loans up to $300. For example, on page VI of the first part the figures are for loans from $100 to $500 and $501 to $1,000 and from $1,001 to $1,500. This makes it extremely difficult to calculate the exact effect of the bill of the hon. member for Assiniboia. For this reason I suggest that the best approach to the bill is to send it to the banking and commerce committee where we could find out

the real effect of the change and the magnitude of what is proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia.
I think the hon. member said on another occasion-I hope he will correct me if I am wrong-that he was not particularly wedded to these figures but that at least he wanted figures substantially lower than the rates that exist at the present time. I think I have given the gist of what he said previously. He nods his head in agreement. With that I can agree. I do think this subject needs another review. There are large areas in which our knowledge could be improved so that we would know exactly what we were getting into. At least with the small loans companies you see the shark for what he is- he is a licensed shark-but if you remove him as a source of credit or as a source of money for people who are in need, then you immediately drive them to people who will make the small loans shark appear almost like a saint by comparison. The problem, without putting haloes on these characters' heads, is to recognize at least there are much worse types of money operators in this country than these people.
Hr. MacGregor's report also gives other interesting information. But, Mr. Speaker, I see I am coming up to six o'clock. I hoped not to be in this particular position because I feel rather strongly on the subject of the bill, as does the hon. member for Assiniboia. Unfortunately, part of the time that I otherwise would have had for speaking was interrupted by a different procedure within this hour.
